FOREIGN TAKEOVERS BILL-SUGGESTED PROVISION FOR MAJORITY OF CANADIANS ON BOARDS OF DIRECTORS AND COMPLIANCE WITH CORPORATE BEHAVIOUR RULES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Industry, Trade and
Commerce. Following the announcement in the Ontario legislature yesterday that the Ontario government intends to take steps to ensure greater Canadian control of foreign-owned firms, and the announcement made yesterday in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs by the chairman of that committee that the minister would be working this weekend on amendments to the foreign takeovers bill, will the minister now assure the House that among the amendments he will bring before us next week will be one to make it mandatory for foreign-owned firms in Canada to have 51 per cent Canadian membership on their boards of directors?

speakeroldname: Hon. lean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: FOREIGN TAKEOVERS BILL-SUGGESTED PROVISION FOR MAJORITY OF CANADIANS ON BOARDS OF DIRECTORS AND COMPLIANCE WITH CORPORATE BEHAVIOUR RULES
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. I explained that. I have given the reason why we thought as a general approach the screening method for takeovers was more realistic and more meaningful than a general automatic rule of Canadian participation. As a government we have explained ourselves fully on that. The hon. member is aware, however, that in Bill C-201, among the factors to be considered in the case of takeovers is Canadian participation, so obviously then participation is not pushed aside as meaningless by the government. What the Premier of Ontario did yesterday shows how right the Prime Minister was when he said that if some provinces feel that Bill C-201 does not go far enough they can always add to it. That is obviously what the Premier of Ontario is doing at this time.

subtopic: FOREIGN TAKEOVERS BILL-SUGGESTED PROVISION FOR MAJORITY OF CANADIANS ON BOARDS OF DIRECTORS AND COMPLIANCE WITH CORPORATE BEHAVIOUR RULES
speechtext: The minister has answered that he does not intend to provide any such 51 per cent requirement. Would he, then, consider another amendment, namely, that all foreign-owned corporations operating in Canada must act in accordance with a fixed set of rules for good corporate behaviour formulated by the federal government, failure to comply with which would result in sanctions?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: FOREIGN TAKEOVERS BILL-SUGGESTED PROVISION FOR MAJORITY OF CANADIANS ON BOARDS OF DIRECTORS AND COMPLIANCE WITH CORPORATE BEHAVIOUR RULES
speechtext:
We already have a set of guidelines for good corporate behaviour, though they do not enjoy the status my hon. friend would like. We have a number of these rules for good corporate behaviour, they were proclaimed in 1967 by one of my predecessors who was then Minister of Trade. These automatic rules by which one prescribes for example 51 per cent of the board of directors must be domiciled in Canada, and so on, are possibly useful rules-I am not denying that-but as I pointed out in the House in the course of my speech on second reading of Bill C-201, it is possible to find ways of getting around these rules and making them, in effect, meaningless. I am not saying they are not useful. I am just saying, as I said previously, that to us the screening method for takeovers is more realistic.

June 16, 1972

friend. subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF AMENDMENTS TO ACT-REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE INQUIRY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subtopic: HIJACKING-CANADIAN POSITION ON REQUEST THAT UNITED NATIONS SECURITY COUNCIL ACT-REQUEST FOR OUTLAWING OF BLACKMAIL PAYMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. What attitude is Canada taking in reference to the prospective submission to the United Nations Security Council of the question of hijacking? What are the expectations of any action being taken by the Security Council having regard to the divided opinion among several members of that council?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: HIJACKING-CANADIAN POSITION ON REQUEST THAT UNITED NATIONS SECURITY COUNCIL ACT-REQUEST FOR OUTLAWING OF BLACKMAIL PAYMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I said in the House of Commons the other day, the Canadian government would be very happy if this matter were brought before the Security Council. We are not members, but in general we have been supporting the idea. We also support action by ICAO, where we are represented, and where we believe that action which might be even more effective could be taken. I think the prospects are not too good, but we are still hopeful that some action will be taken because we would like some declaration by the United Nations or its principal agency that hijacking must be dealt with effectively and enlisting the support of all countries to deal effectively with hijackers by making sure they are brought to justice.

subtopic: HIJACKING-CANADIAN POSITION ON REQUEST THAT UNITED NATIONS SECURITY COUNCIL ACT-REQUEST FOR OUTLAWING OF BLACKMAIL PAYMENTS
speechtext: Whether or not the Security Council will act, of course, is very problematical, and it is almost impossible to anticipate favourable action. Having regard to the fact that there are deep fears of hijacking among passengers using aircraft in Canada and that each nation should take individual action in that international action is difficult, will the minister give consideration to having brought before the House before the adjournment an amendment to the law to provide that ransom or blackmail payments shall not be paid, thereby removing the incentive of the highly attractive remunerative opportunities which seem available to hijackers today?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: HIJACKING-CANADIAN POSITION ON REQUEST THAT UNITED NATIONS SECURITY COUNCIL ACT-REQUEST FOR OUTLAWING OF BLACKMAIL PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I ought to preface my answer to that question by saying that Canada will be ratifying the international convention on hijacking now that the legislation has been approved. I expect this will be done on Monday. I have signed the necessary papers.
As to the second question of whether one can effectively legislate against blackmail, this is a problem with which the right hon. gentleman, I am sure, has been familiar in his practice. I think it is virtually impossible to prevent people from making payments in order to save the lives of those they love.

subtopic: HIJACKING-CANADIAN POSITION ON REQUEST THAT UNITED NATIONS SECURITY COUNCIL ACT-REQUEST FOR OUTLAWING OF BLACKMAIL PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are many laws that are virtually incapable of full enforcement, but does the minister not consider that the removal of the incentive of potential gain under the law would certainly reduce the probability of many hijacking operations such as are taking place today? Would the minister say whether this matter has ever been considered instead of giving an offhand opinion such as the one he has just given?

June 16, 1972
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
This House regrets the Government's continuing refusal to this date to intervene in the impasse between the International Longshoremen's Association and the Maritime Employers' Association despite the short and long term damage to the St. Lawrence seaports, to the users of the national transportation system and to the economic well-being of Canada and despite the sufferings of the longshoremen and their families; and therefore this House, in the public interest, calls upon the Government to intervene forthwith to end the strike.
Mr. Speaker, before dealing with the matter which I have brought before the House this morning as a motion, I would like to invite the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) who is directly involved and responsible to the House for the administration of legislation regarding working conditions in Canada and for disputes which
June 16, 1972

may concern the federal government directly or indirectly.
I wish the Minister of Labour were present in the House but in his absence, the former Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) at least should be here as Acting Minister of Labour, because when disputes cannot be settled by the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration is often asked to step in. I am truly disappointed to see that neither of those ministers are present to reply to a most important question.
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to start a useless quarrel but rather to acknowledge the unfortunate situation which prevails in Canada due to a most serious problem affecting thousands of workers and the Canadian economy.

First of all, the refusal-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have clearly said that I do not wish to associate this very important matter with this sort of pranks played by some members and I regret that the hon. member does not take seriously so serious a question as that which we are discussing this morning.
Mr. Speaker, the motion contains five major items: First, the refusal by the government to break the deadlock through some positive action; second, the short and longterm damage to the St. Lawrence ports; third, the damage to the users of the national transportation system; fourth, the damage to the economic well-being of Canada and, by implication, of Montreal and Quebec; fifth, the human aspect involved in the hardship of the longshoremen and their families.
Representing a constituency which is at the heart of Montreal harbour activity and where a very substantial number of longshoremen involved in the dispute live, I had to intervene to protect the interests of my constituents and of the people of Canada as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec City have been paralysed for more than 30 days because of a conflict involving both the shipping firms and the longshoremen which only a few weeks ago had come to an agreement whereby the former Minister of Labour and member for Verdun would insure order in the ports for at least the next three years. Now, both parties find themselves right back where they started about their collective agreement with all the efforts made by both sides to come to a satisfactory agreement wasted.
An exact description of this situation was recently published as an editorial in the June 5, 1972 issue of Le Journal de Montreal, editorial which I wish to quote for the accuracy of its insight. In this editorial, Mr. Paul Gros d'Aillon puts the problems in its proper perspective before public opinion, and I quote:
3208

June 16, 1972
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
The conflict is so pointless, so subtle that no one really knows how to interpret it. No one knows either who is wrong or who is right. The employers interpreted in their own way the terms of the labour agreement on the constitution of the unloading crews. The union members countered and quit work. The employer retaliated and everyone was fired. The courts before which the case stands wonder what to do and the federal department of Labour refuses to grant the employers in the three ports of the St. Lawrence the right to take the longshoremen's union before the courts.
Arbitration should therefore be resorted to, to settle the conflict, but both sides attempt to lose themselves in a judicial jungle which camouflages the basic truths of the problem. In other words, no one will budge.
There is the gist of the problem, Mr. Speaker. Both parties are watching who is going to make the first move. In spite of the fact that either party, or both, would do well to go to arbitration, there is an accepted procedure which is contained in the collective agreement that was signed on March 29, 1972 and which is in force until December 31, 1974. This is indicated in paragraph 11 of section 1 and more specifically in paragraph 5, concerning grievance procedures.
However, as the editorial writer said, it is a matter of no one wanting to budge.
Notwithstanding this procedure provided in the collective agreement in cases of grievances, none of the interested parties has indicated its willingness to use it so far. This is ridiculous and unjustifiable.
It is a matter of mutual "pouting", Mr. Speaker, between the parties concerned, where the government and the Minister of Labour find themselves in a moral and political obligation to intervene in this conflict.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will certainly limit my remarks to the matter under study, as I feel the latter to be far too important for anybody to waste the time of this House in replies and exchanges of that kind.
I was talking, Mr. Speaker, of a conflict which is extremely serious. I spoke about the points which I raised in the motion. There are five of them, and it seems to me that they are clear. I concluded by saying that the only solution which seems practicable to solve this conflict at present, to put an end to the deadlock, is to take it to arbitration.
Mr. Speaker, if this was only my suggestion, I think that some hon. members would have the right to challenge this conclusion. But this solution, which seems to be the only feasible one at present, does not come from me alone. I have also consulted newspapers and certain reports, certain statements by responsible men whose advice has been taken in previous strikes-among which the former Minister of Labour, the hon. member for Verdun, who recently said, concerning this strike, that the only solution left was arbitration. It is reported in the newspaper Montreal-Matin of Wednesday, May 24, 1972, that the hon. member for Verdun, the former Minister of Labour, was behind the signing of the collective agreement between the shipowners and the longshoremen. The hon. member for Verdun is reported as saying that arbitration was most advisable under the circumstances.
Last night, Mr. Speaker-whether the hon. member for St. Boniface likes it or not-the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who is on a tour in Labrador City, made some very
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
interesting statements. An article in today's issue of Montreal-Matin reads as follows:
-Mr. Trudeau replied that it would be a very good idea indeed, and that arbitration should be extended to all activities, "because, he said, strike is a last resort, somewhat similar to war. Eventually, everybody loses by it."
Then, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister himself is in favour of arbitration to settle disputes of that kind.
This morning also, during an interview on a Quebec radio network, the Quebec Minister of Labour accused the federal government of failing to do anything in this dispute between ship-owners and longshoremen. Mr. Cournoyer, Minister of Labour in Mr. Bourassa's Liberal government said that if the federal government was not going to do anything about it, the provincial Minister of Labour will have to intervene even if that dispute does not come directly under the jurisdiction of the provincial government. Mr. Cournoyer blamed the incapacity, the "wait and see" policy and the inaction of the federal Minister of Labour, because he is concerned just as we are about the disastrous effects of any extension of such a strike on the general economic activity in the province of Quebec. He also said that if the federal Minister of Labour did not settle the conflict, he would have to interfere himself.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, whenever such a situation develops, the matter is serious enough, I believe, for the federal government to get involved in the settling of the dispute. They should get involved because the former Minister of Labour, the hon. member for Verdun, did have his say in the drafting of the collective agreement between the longshoremen and the ship-owners.
Mr. Speaker, the minister answered various questions in this House on that subject. He said among other things that he could not intervene, that the collective agreement provided for arbitration, and that both parties had to comply with regulations. Now in answer to a question directed to him, the minister said that the Maritime Employers' Union was prepared to accept arbitration, but that it had not yet started the procedure to that effect.
On the other hand, it is reported that the longshoremen are also prepared to go to arbitration, but that they do not want to initiate it.
Here is the crux of the matter, Mr. Speaker. The problem is that according to an established procedure, if a dispute arises between the two parties, it must be settled through arbitration, but neither party wants arbitration. Then how should the government or the public get this problem solved?
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have here the collective agreement which was signed on March 29th, 1972. I shall quote now article 1.11:
Should a conflict arise concerning new methods of work, the loading or unloading of ships or any related operation that affects the health or security of the workers, the parties shall meet to solve the dispute, and failing an agreement, it shall be submitted to arbitration according to the procedure set out in other provisions of this agreement.
Now, for the information of the members, I point out that the other provisions are seriously involved in the
25319-17J

June 16, 1972
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike problem, as one realizes on reading the introduction to the chapter entitled "Grievance procedure". I quote:
Any disagreement as to interpretation or application of the present agreement is a grievance as defined within the agreement. Grievances are settled according to the following procedure-
If the grievance committee fails to settle the grievance within the five (5) following working days, the grievance shall be submitted to a sole mediator, chosen in conformity with the present agreement. The mediator shall render his decision within the seven (7) following working days, or within a longer period agreed upon by the parties.
Paragraph (d) deals with requests for arbitration, which I consider to be interesting because this is where we find the provisions actually related to the conflict. I quote that paragraph:
The request for arbitration can be filed either by the Union or by the Maritime Employers Association. The party making the request for arbitration shall make a written outline of the conflict submitted for arbitration and send copy thereof to the other party.
In the present dispute, neither of the parties has filed an application for arbitration with the other party. Each side stands by its position. The collective agreement also provides for who can act as an arbitrator in case of a dispute.
Paragraph (d) in the same section reads as follows:
The single arbitrator shall be selected from the following list: 1. The honourable Chief Justice A. B. Gold; 2. Hon. Justice Elphege Marier; 3. Hon. Justice Jacques Vadboncoeur, and 4. Mr. Raymond Leboeuf, barrister.
It is agreed that the arbitrator designated by the parties on any occasion shall be available Mondays to Fridays-
These are matters of detail, but what is important is the provision in paragraph (f) of section 5, which reads as follows:
In case the arbitrators referred to in the above paragraph should be unable to act, the arbitrator shall be chosen by the parties or, in the absence of an agreement, by the federal Minister of Labour.
In fact, we can read clearly here that the Minister of Labour and the federal government are involved in the grievance procedure concerning a dispute such as this one which now opposes the longshoremen of St. Lawrence ports and the shippers.
If the contracting parties cannot agree on the choice of an arbitrator-I understand that the arbitrator is involved-it is stated that the federal government, through the Minister of Labour, must intervene to designate him.
Now Mr. Speaker, since we are faced with two entirely antagonistic parties which have never expressed the wish to meet, in_ my opinion, it goes without saying that the federal Minister of Labour, according to the spirit and letter of that clause, could and should intervene in case of disagreement.
Mr. Speaker, I do not at all understand why each time that some conflict has risen with serious consequences for Quebec, especially for the Montreal area as well as for the entire Canadian economy, the minister has fallen into the nasty way of taking refuge by saying: The minister cannot interfere, the parties must get together and come to an agreement. We cannot interfere.
[Mr. Valade.l
Unless this negative attitude is reversed, I wonder, Mr. Speaker, how long it will take before a solution is found to this problem.
In my view, the former Minister of Labour, when he spoke to the House in 1966 regarding harbour difficulties involving the same parties was not saying the same thing. It would certainly be most interesting to read some statements that the hon. member for Verdun made on June 7, 1966, as the then Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour concerning the conflict existing at the port of Montreal. The hon. member for Verdun was then answering the liberal member for Trois-Rivieres, the late Mr. J.-A. Mongrain, who was asking the federal government to intervene in this conflict. The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, for whom I had a lot of admiration and respect, said when asking the minister to intervene in the dispute at the port of Montreal, and I quote:
In view of the disastrous circumstances of the present longshoremen's strike, should the minister not take drastic and extraordinary steps so that the activity will be resumed while negotiations are under way?
The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres was making these comments in the House on account of that strike.
And the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour, the hon. member for Verdun, now Minister of Manpower and Immigration, who was also at one time Minister of Labour and who had drafted the collective agreement, replied to the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres as follows:
I noted . .. the very intelligent remarks of the hon. member for Three Rivers-
He had just talked about compulsory arbitration-And further the hon. member for Verdun said:
At the same time I realize, as do I am sure most members of the house, that some extraordinary measures will eventually have to be taken if this longshoremen's strike is to be brought to a satisfactory conclusion.
Those were the remarks made by the then Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour, who became later Minister of Labour and who is now Minister of Manpower and Immigration. He said in the House that extraordinary measures would have to be taken to find a solution to the longshoremen's dispute.
The situation that prevails at this time, Mr. Speaker, is almost identical to the one existing then, except that it is more urgent now, since this dispute is in its fifth week and there is no end in sight. It will soon enter in its sixth week.
Mr. Speaker, the economic implications of this strike, the effects of this deadlock on the future of the Quebec ports are obviously disastrous. One could talk of immediate and long term implications of the situation on the economy at all levels: national and local, on the future life of the St. Lawrence ports, on the families of employees who are suffering from this strike.
It is well known that harbour activities on the St. Lawrence River are the most important industry in Quebec. The port of Montreal, being the largest in the system, is more directly and strongly affected.
June 16, 1972

Moreover, this conflict has arisen in the most active part of the season, that is the months of May, June and July. Under normal circumstances, the port of Montreal can count on the presence to at least 125 to 150 ships at this time of the year. There were merely 7 of them a few days ago.
A good number of ships have returned to their port of departure or were rerouted. Some of them have been able to drop anchor in the ports of Toronto, Halifax and St. John's. But these harbours having limited facilities, many ships have set sail toward American ports. Montreal will have lost to date some 525,000 tons of cargo including
225,000	of general merchandise which is the main source of direct tax income for the federal government.
Some importers have advised their suppliers to refrain from shipping cargo via Montreal.
Some important shipowners such as McLean Kennedy Limited and Furness Withy & Co. Ltd., have already moved their harbour facilities from Montreal to Halifax.
Will shippers who, in spite of the last dockers' strike had once again relied on the St. Lawrence harbours, sever their ties with Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec? Some business circles fear this possibility.
Mr. Speaker, if we were seeking to permanently destroy the harbour system which is still vital for the maintenance of Quebec's economic prosperity, we would not act differently.
It would be right to seriously ask oneself this question in the face of a situation that was literally and wilfully left to deteriorate.
The slightest permanent decrease in harbour activities at Montreal, Trois-Rivieres or Quebec that this conflict might entail, would cause not only serious gaps in the local economy but would also be a grave threat to the jobs of thousands of workers directly or indirectly linked with harbour services.
The laissez-faire or wait-and-see policy of the government, and particularly the Minister of Labour, demonstrates such unawareness of the disastrous consequences of this situation that we must denounce it most vigorously.
The predecessor of the present Minister of Labour, the hon. member for Verdun, would certainly not have taken this matter so lightly, had he still been in office. It is unfortunate that the considerable efforts made by the hon. member for Verdun at the time when he was Minister of Labour in order to achieve the signing of the collective agreement last March have failed to ensure the promised stability.
This conflict will have a serious impact on the national economy, as the government will be deprived of the substantial revenues derived from operations in Quebec harbours.
In fact, in 1970 and 1971, the government received over $329 million yearly in direct revenues under the customs and excise acts.
Harbour operations are therefore an extremely important economic generator which the minister cannot afford to ignore, especially in the difficult times which we are going through in Canada, and particularly in Quebec, at present.
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
It is estimated that every ton of goods handled in harbours represents an economic generation factor of between $12 and $14 per capita.
Over the last five years, operations in Quebec harbours have provided the government with revenues of $3.5 billion.
Now, it is clearly urgent for the government to take the necessary steps in order to resolve this conflict, not only because of its serious impact on the Canadian economy and the future of the St. Lawrence harbours, but above all because of the human problems which afflict the employees concerned and their families.
I said in my opening remarks that I represent a constituency which is particularly affected by this strike. I had occasion to meet with longshoremen who told me of their concern over the situation, which does not seem about to be settled.
They made me understand the difficulties their families had to face as a result of the strike, for we all know that with this conflict, the families of longshoremen on strike cannot count on social welfare-since they cannot get it under the provincial law-nor on unemployment insurance benefits, since the unemployment insurance act has no provision concerning these conditions. They are not entitled to any other relief funds, which means that the affectef families are most depressed and they can only expect to get assistance from a few benevolent societies, like the Societe Saint-Vincent-de-Paul and other organizations of this kind.

speechtext:
What the hon. member says in his motion is that the government should intervene forthwith to end the strike. I must say that if he has in mind steps to put this matter before the courts, then we would disagree. If he has in mind some sort of strike breaking action-though it is a little difficult to use that phrase because it is not a strike, it is a lock-out- again we would disagree. I see the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) disagrees with what I am saying about the dispute being a lockout, but there we are. If the hon. member has in mind calling upon the government to bring in legislation to put these employees back to work, the employees who may not be employees because they have been suspended, we do not agree with that either.
I know there is a great deal of current feeling about strikes, about unions and about workers, and I understand it, particularly when it affects the public generally.
June 16, 1972

But let us not forget that the sanctity of the law and the sacredness of rights must include protecting the law at all times and protecting those rights which have been established in a society such as ours. The right of employers and employees to disagree and to carry that disagreement to the point of a stoppage of work is one of the factors of our society. We have had to live with this for a long time. Someone may come up with a better way and he will be a great hero when he does. In the meantime, we do not aid the cause of amity or industrial peace in our society simply by putting the blame on trade unions, on workers and on strikers. Neither do we solve the problem by making generalized speeches for 30 minutes calling upon the government to intervene and end it without saying what the government should do.
I intend to be very brief. One or more of my colleagues may speak later in the day and, if they do, they, too, will be brief. There is the suggestion that has come from the National Farmers Union that if there is no solution for some time to this matter the government might consider taking over the operations, putting them under an administrator or something until an agreement can be reached. That point will be put forward later, but we contend that even that should not be proposed until a serious effort has been made by the Minister of Labour along the lines he is already following.
If we have a quarrel with the Minister of Labour, and I speak for my leader who happens to be away today, and for the rest of us in this party, it is not with the nature of what he is doing, it is with the degree and the vigour of it. He said the other day in response to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) that he was doing his best to get the two parties to have regard for their obligations to each other. Then, he used this sentence:
That kind of intervention I have indeed pursued vigorously.
He looks at me and seems to be asking if I want him to be more vigorous. That is right. Later on that same day, Wednesday, June 14, we find another response to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis). The sentence I have read was from page 3124 of Hansard. Looking over at page 3125, I find this response at the end of a series of questions:
I would point out that the two parties themselves appointed the arbitrators and that four arbitrators are named in the agreement. The initiative falls on one or the other of the two parties. They each have the obligation.
I agree with the minister's statement as a description of the situation as it obtains legally, but the public interest is involved in all of this and it is the job of the Minister of Labour to represent that public interest. Our suggestion, our plea and our urging to him is that he regard what he has called vigorous in the past as not vigorous enough, and that he make every effort he possibly can to get the two parties together in a place they choose, or let him choose the place, and stay with the two parties hour upon hour, day upon day, night upon night if necessary until they either reach an agreement or until they agree to send the matter to arbitration. Our suggestion is as simple as that. We are not asking for legislation. In fact, we do not want it. We are not asking for police action and we are not asking for the matter to be taken to the courts. We are trying to avoid the mistake I think the last member made
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
in calling for something to be done and not saying what he meant.
I almost have to say that in a sense I like the stance of the Minister of Labour in respecting the law and the rights of both sides. We appreciate the fact that he appreciates the rights of the workers and I cannot quarrel with his respecting the rights of the employers as well. That is the way it has to be. Unfortunately for him, as a new Minister of Labour trying to find his way in this important area, he has this problem on his hands and we think there is no other reasonable and decent solution to it but the one we are suggesting, namely that he do everything he can, and that does not mean legal action or throwing his weight around as a minister of the government who would have the power to bring in legislation, but rather as the Minister of Labour, to get these people together in an appropriate room in an appropriate place somewhere and say: Boys, we are staying here until this matter is settled. Let the government pay the cost of the room and provide the meals when keeping them there until, for their own sake, for the sake of the families of those involved and for the sake of the economy of the country, this matter is settled.
I say again, Sir, we are not asking the minister to adopt in nature something he is not now doing. He has talked to both sides, but we are asking him to carry this to its ultimate conclusion by actually getting both parties together and keeping them there until they, under his guidance and direction, settle this dispute for the good of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that earlier I objected to the hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade), who is the mover, continuing his remarks because allegedly he wanted to submit solutions. He had exactly 40 minutes, I believe, to submit them, and he did not put them to good use. It was not my intention to prevent him from submitting solutions, but to prevent him from taking up the time of other hon. members.
Mr. Speaker, I rather endorse the views expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg-North-Centre (Mr. Knowles) to the effect that the minister should meet the two parties involved, because public interest is at stake and settlement does not concern merely shipowners and longshoremen, but a a great many people involved in trucking, business, etc. Moreover, there are people who have been expecting goods from Japan and other countries for nearly a month and a half and cannot get them.
So, in the interest of the community and the people as a whole, the minister must give orders, meet the leaders of the International Longshoremen's Association and the representatives of management and bring them together around a table to discuss the problem.
Not only the strike is at issue. I can understand the situation on both sides. Wednesday morning, I was in Montreal, speaking on Mr. Jarraud's program on CKVL and a longshoreman called me. He was almost crying while describing the terrible situation in which the longshoremen find themselves at present and he told me that

June 16, 1972
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
this whole dispute could have been avoided from the beginning in less than 24 hours if only the parties had been willing to meet.
But nobody would give in. The union leader, Mr. Saint-Onge, refuses to meet the employers, saying that they have bent the provisions of the collective agreement stipulating that the computers will be used as of September and not May. Now, the use of the computers started as early as may, which did not please Mr. Saint-Onge.
However, that his was not the only thing that started the dispute. Before this long one, there was a one-day dispute and that was not provided for in the collective agreement. It was decided to strike on that day to support the famous Quebec Common Front of labour unions, but Mr. Saint-Onge does not talk about that. True, the collective agreement contains provisions for the use of computers as early as September, but their use, since May, has not prejudiced those who were working in the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec City.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, one must be honest and straightforward, and call a spade a spade. There are lots of problems, and not only on the ship-owners' side, but also on the longshoremen's side.
I was even told by a docker that some workers steal boats, motorcycles, radios and television sets. The insurance companies have to refund the price of the goods stolen in the ports along the St. Lawrence river.
That is not provided or in the collective agreement; yet, such is the practice. The union leaders do not mention that. Mr. Saint-Onge did not refer to it. However, he is always criticizing the employer, the ship-owner, and so on.
Not long ago, a $2 million loan was suggested with a view to replenishing the strike fund of the Montreal dockers. As for me, I say to fellows like Saint-Onge et al. Why not be honest about it? Instead of borrowing $2 million to replenish the strike fund and telling the longshoremen that they will continue to get $20 or $25 a week even if they do not work, why not buy ships and become shipowners and treat the workers as they would like to be treated? But no. They borrow to go on strike. They do not have the courage to borrow to build something.
Mr. Speaker, the problem is difficult but still a solution is possible. Arbitration is necessary at this point. One of the shipowners is willing to go to arbitration, but the union leaders will not hear of it.
That is why, in the name of the common good, of the public interest, the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) should intervene. Even then, the shipowners should not be kept from going to court to establish who is right or wrong in this case, and arrive at a judgment or decision that would let us know where we are going.
This morning, the radio announced that the Quebec Minister of Labour had bluntly stated this: If Ottawa does not get a move on, Quebec will.
And because this matter comes under federal jurisdiction, the Minister of Labour told us yesterday that he could do nothing more, that all they have to do is negotiate or request an arbitrator, The minister will not assume his responsibility in this respect.

This morning, his Quebec counterpart stated: This is none of my business but since the federal government will not take any action, I shall do so in its place. And he offered his services.
This is why I claim that it is the minister's imperative duty to obtain that both parties come to the bargaining table or accept arbitration, in order to end this disastrous strike, because neither the union leaders nor the employers will provide for the wives and children of the Montreal longshoremen. At the present time, there is undeserved misery in Montreal, and everybody complains about it, including the mothers.
A trucker called to tell me: We might lose our trucks since we cannot meet our payments because the strike prevents us from working. A whole group of people is in the same situation and mainly small businessmen who fear bankruptcy because of this disastrous strike.
And Wednesday morning after I was interviewed on television, someone asked me: What is the federal government waiting for to do something and reach a decision? All the Montreal longshoremen are waiting for this.
Let nobody think that all longshoremen approve their union leaders' statements. Last Monday morning, it was a shame to see the longshoremen gathered at the Paul Sauve centre in Montreal willing to go back to work, while another group insisted on picketing. And labourers working on the same sites were fighting like cats and dogs and tried to break each others legs. Why? For the common good? No. They do not even know why. They fight each other when they need to cooperate in order to obtain justice for everyone.
Unfortunately, many union leaders disagree on this point. Since some employers have also been unfair to the workers, this proves that both parties are to blame, but it is not by keeping them apart that we will get satisfactory results.
That is why it is imperative for the minister to take action and not to allow himself to be outdone by his Quebec counterpart. It would be funny if we heard tonight that the Quebec Minister of Labour (Mr. Cournoy-er) had a meeting with the shipowners and labour leaders this afternoon and that it had been decided to put an end to the dispute. The responsible federal minister would look a little foolish, and I will be watching him on Monday to see if that has happened. In the meantime, however, I would ask whether it would be possible for him to see these people over the weekend and arrange for a meeting.
As far as the computer quarrel is concerned, I cannot accept that is very logical. Perhaps some conditions of the collective agreement have not been observed because of the use of computers in May to decide whether the services of 8 men instead of 10 or 16 would be needed according to the ship's tonnage.
Whether computers are used in May or September is of no serious consequences. However, under the terms of the collective agreement, they are to be used in September. This is a case where the shipowners have not observed their part of the agreement.
June 16, 1972

On the other hand, employees have been told: You will not be replaced until September. In this case, the labour leaders have no reasons to get excited because nobody is losing his job.
Mr. Speaker, this is the serious situation in which the longshoremen find themselves and which is affecting the economy of the entire province as well as that of the rest of Canada.
I repeat that I am in favour of unions, but the Montreal maritime unions are members of an international association. How can there be talk of union solidarity when ships are being turned away from Montreal so that they will be unloaded along the American seaboard by members of the same association? Talk about solidarity!
Mr. Speaker, the longshoremen in the province of Quebec, along the St. Lawrence river, understand the situation and are eager to see this dispute come to an end. If some union leaders and ship-owners do not see it that way, the minister has the responsibility of saying: Come and negotiate immediately so that we may end this dispute, have the longshoremen return to work and restore some order in this very important field of economic activities for the benefit of our whole country and in particular for the benefit of the province of Quebec.
Here are the remarks, Mr. Speaker, that I wanted to make today; there is only one solution, in my opinion, under the circumstances: the minister must take action.
The minister recently replied to my colleague the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) that he had prevented the ship-owners from prosecuting the union because there were other ways to settle the dispute. Now six weeks have elapsed and the other means have not produced results because nothing has been done so far, whereas an injunction or proceedings might have solved the problem by now.
So I should like to know today what means, what solutions the government has in mind or intends to bring forward to settle that labour dispute that has already lasted six weeks and should not have happened.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, labour-management relations at the port of Montreal have been a source of trouble since the early 1960's. They have been the subject of special industrial inquiries and, in 1966, of special legislation. Under my predecessor, working conditions at the port of Montreal were substantially improved. An important collective agreement was reached in 1968 with great difficulty. This was followed by continuous efforts to improve the climate of labour-management relations on the docks.
Ports throughout Europe were visited by representatives of both parties, assisted by the federal Department of Labour. Some eight months of constant and intensive mediation, led by two senior officers of my department, culminated in the collective agreement reached in April, 1972, just a few short months ago, an agreement ratified by an overwhelming majority of the union membership. Mr. Speaker, this is not an ordinary collective agreement. Its provisions promise to set labour-management relations on the docks at Montreal on an entirely new course. They
3216

June 16, 1972
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
promise to set the port of Montreal in the forefront of world ports. This agreement coped with the impact on dock workers of the rapid technological changes which have come about at docks all over the world in the methods of working ships, in loading and unloading, in the use of mechanized equipment.
This agreement provided very significant inprovements in pension benefits. It coped with job security of longshoremen with a guarantee of 37 weeks of pay per annum, and it provided for the new and essential levels of productivity required by the employers to pay the enhanced benefits to the workers and to attract and hold business in the port of Montreal. Increased productivity levels required the break up of established work gang systems, and the introduction of new methods of work assignment related to the introduction of a computer. Productivity by the men was the exchange for the job security and the pension and wage benefits. That was a breakthrough in industrial relations at this port.
Throughout the period from 1962 to 1972, eight major work stoppages and five lesser strikes occurred on the Montreal docks, involving in the major instances between
2,000	and 4,000 workers and lasting from one day to well over a month. Why and how did the present dispute arise, and what is the basic nature of the present dispute? The basic issue which precipitated this particular dispute- and I want to stress that it is a dispute which is part of a series which have disrupted the Montreal docks over the past decade-was whether or not management, under the new agreement, at this time had the right to break up longshore gangs prior to the introduction of the computer dispatch system to be inaugurated by mid-September.
Management took the initiative of breaking up a gang working a hatch and ordered some members of the gang to work in a shed. The International Longshoremen's Union contends that management does not have this right until the introduction of the computer dispatch system. While this is the basic issue, other issues have subsequently arisen. The suspension of longshoremen by the Maritime Employers' Association and the question of the collective agreement are examples of additional issues. However, in a nutshell, these are the basic issues in dispute and, without going into all their complexities, I may say that additional issues have become involved in disputes of this nature.
It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to comment on the position of the parties or to enter into any debate on the merit of the position of either party, as this involves interpretation of the collective agreement. I have repeatedly said that there is a provision in the collective agreement, as the law requires, for either or both of the parties to put this question of interpretation into arbitration, that is, to arbitrate it.
May I pause at this point and respond to some of the remarks hon. members have made in interpreting this matter. It has been said that I have condoned the decision taken by the Lonshoremen's Union. I did not condone that decision; I did not endorse it. The longshoremen had a remedy, which was to go to arbitration. The law gave the longshoremen no right to engage in an illegal work stop-

page. I do not agree with those who say this is a lockout. Those questions are not the important ones that we must settle in this House. The root questions we are concerned with are the remedies provided by law and the use that must be made cf those remedies if we are to sustain the collective bargaining system in Canada rather than undermine it by rescuing those who will not adhere to their obligations.
The procedures, Mr. Speaker, are crystal clear and there are no questions concerning procedures to be followed in this particular instance. They are clear in the Canada Labour Code and clearly set out in the collective agreement that was signed by both parties one year ago. Section 125(1) of the Canada Labour Code provides:
Every collective agreement shall contain a provision for final settlement without stoppage of work, by arbitration or otherwise, of all differences between the parties to or persons bound by the agreement or on whose behalf it was entered into, concerning its meaning or violation.
Subsection (3) of that section provides:
Every party to and every person bound by the agreement, and every person on whose behalf the agreement was entered into, shall comply with the provision for final settlement contained in the agreement and give effect thereto.
Let us turn for a moment to the collective agreement affecting those who, over a period of time, have brought the Port of Montreal into the forefront of the world's ports. What did the parties agree to? They agreed that they would take their grievances over interpretation of their agreement and their disagreements over the interpretation of those provisions to arbitrators whom they had the foresight to name in the agreement. Four arbitrators stand by ready to respond to the application of either party for the arbitration of differences. Paragraph (d) of article (5) of the collective agreement sets out the situation where the union or the employer wishes to submit a matter to arbitration. It provides that either party may initiate a request for arbitration. The parties requesting the arbitrator must set out in writing the matter submitted to the arbitrator and send a copy of it to the other party. Paragraph (h) of that article in the agreement provides that the arbitrator's decision shall be final and binding. Paragraph (i) provides that the men are to return to work pending completion of arbitration procedures.
Perhaps I ought to pause here. Let us ask ourselves, what is the value of an arbitration procedure? What role does it play in collective bargaining in Canada? It plays a unique role, an extremely important role, in Canada; and here the situation with respect to collective bargaining is unique. Once an agreement is concluded and the contract is signed, that agreement is closed, if I may use the expression which is current, and it cannot be broken by strikes or lockouts.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
Work stoppages during the period of a closed agreement are not legal. Once you close an agreement in fashion in Canada, a work stoppage is not legal. There are no parallel agreements which are closed in other countries. The agreements are not the same in the United States, where lockouts and strikes may occur. Of course, during the closed period of an agreement, most frequently the parties concerned waive rights to strike or
June 16, 1972

lockout voluntarily, but in Canada this is the law. Once an agreement is signed and sealed, it is closed.
How is relief provided with respect to disagreements, if one is to make strikes and lockouts illegal for a two or three year period. There must be provision for some relief, because grievances will arise and differences in interpretation will arise. It is the role of the arbitrator to provide relief and the parties agree that, in exchange for stability during that period of the closed contract, they will arbitrate their differences. The statute requires that they do that. If any collective agreement does not include within it any provision for arbitration, the Canada Labour Relations Board may prescribe an arbitration proceeding and this will be deemed to be part of that agreement. So, we can see in Canada how extremely significant is that arbitration proceeding. It is there to ventilate grievances and to settle differences during this closed period and is a concept which both labour and management in Canada have accepted and supported for 30 years. It would be an extreme step if anyone were to attempt to undermine the arbitration procedure, and to set it aside, if the parties will not willingly make use of it but wish to use another proceeding. That would be a precedent which would strike at the very root of the system of free, collective bargaining, as practised in Canada.
I repeat, these arbitration procedures are crystal clear. There is no question about them. The arbitrators are named, the obligations are there and I and my officials have repeatedly instructed the parties to follow those procedures. As I understand it, the hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade) intended to propose to the House-I regret that his time ran out before he had an opportunity to make his suggestion-that the Canada Labour Code should be amended so that the minister may impose arbitration on parties unwilling to obey laws already existing.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have underlined the extreme importance to the system of collective bargaining in Canada of the arbitration provisions. Are there alternatives? It has been suggested that mediation should take place. There is a place for mediation in collective bargaining. Its proper place is in the open period when the parties are negotiating.
In this particular case, I have already referred to the intensive effort over many months to bring these parties together to improve the climate of their relationships. But to mediate a grievance dispute is an entirely different matter. Mediation normally takes place over interest disputes; conditions of work, questions of pay, holidays and technological change. These are matters of interest to the parties, but once the agreement is signed and a grievance arises they are not mediated by a mediator. The grievance dispute is settled by an arbitration procedure which is binding on both parties and fundamental to keeping the contract closed. If we set aside mediation, we are in effect opening the agreement and saying, "change it, mediate". We are saying to one party or another to a dispute, if you hang that is tough. If you take illegal action or if you refuse to use the legal proceedings, the arbitration proceedings, then at some point the public interest will be so engaged that you will be taken off the hook. That is the way to underline collective bargaining in Canada.
You can go across this country and you will find that trade unions and management will support the arbitration proceedings and will stand firm against a mediation process that undermines that. It is said by some that mediation is a last resort. A last resort comes when everything else has been tried. The point here is that the proper
3218

June 16, 1972
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
procedures have not been tried. It is open to the parties to try them. I ask them to come to their senses and make use of those provisions that are in their own agreements which they only recently and solemnly agreed to honour.
There are other alternatives open to the parties. If the parties wish to mediate that is up to them, but there are hazards to mediation initiated from outside. In the first instance, it must be appreciated that arbitration of such disputes is required by law. In the second instance, mediation is totally dependent upon voluntary participation by the parties concerned and cannot be a substitution for the provisions of the law. To mediate such a dispute, even in the event that the parties agreed to such an approach, would establish a precedent by giving recognition to mediation as a substitute or alternative to the law in such circumstances.
One of the cornerstones of sound industrial relations is the fact that parties to a collective agreement should settle, through the grievance and arbitration procedures of their collective agreement, any disputes which arise as to the meaning of an agreement they freely entered into. A departure from this concept, based in law, through the provision of mediation services by the Department of Labour, is fraught with danger and could lead to difficulties. It would invite both labour and management to avoid the grievance and arbitration procedures where it suited their particular interest of the moment, and would encourage illegal work stoppages. Responsible officers in labour and management who have to cope with day-today contract administration would take a very serious view of any initiative by the Minister of Labour which would set a precedent whereby disputes involving interpretation of a collective agreement would be subject to mediation.
Where management and labour are dissatisfied with any particular provision of a collective agreement they have entered into for a set term, there is a remedy under Section 126 of the Canada Labour Code. Subsection 2 reads:
Nothing in this Section prevents the revision of any provision of a collective agreement other than the provision relating to the term of the collective agreement that under the agreement is subject to revision during the term thereof.
If the two parties do not wish or will not use the arbitration proceedings, it is open to them to change provisions of the agreement if they mutually agree to do so. Another alternative exists. It is not one that I recommend. However, it has been suggested that an industrial inquiry commission be established. Under Section 159 of the Canada Labour Code, the minister may, either upon application or of his own initiative, appoint an industrial inquiry commission to inquire into industrial matters, and such a commission may make recommendations to secure industrial peace and to promote conditions favourable to settlement of disputes.
Such commissions have been appointed in the past, but not in a situation where the dispute involves interpretation of the collective agreement and where a remedy is provided to the parties through the grievance and arbitration procedures in the collective agreement. Commissions take time. The appointment of an industrial inquiry commission does not ensure resumption of work unless the

parties agree to resume operations while the industrial inquiry commission hears the dispute. In the current situation involving the Quebec ports, this would require not only an assurance by the union that the employees would return to work, but it would also require the Maritime Employers' Association to lift the suspension placed on the employees. If the parties jointly request the Minister of Labour to appoint an industrial inquiry commission with the assurance that there will be a resumption of operations in the St. Lawrence ports, the minister will give immediate consideration to such a request.
In summary, let me say that the remedies are crystal clear. They are open to the parties. I have expressed willingness at any time to meet with the parties to this dispute, provided that will serve a useful purpose and will not be taken by either party as turning back the clock in order that either of the parties may succeed in disrupting the port and then ask the government to take action. Those who say the government should settle that dispute by certain means, by legislation or mediation or trusteeship are wide of the mark. I set my face against those who would propose those measures at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
What is at stake? It is not only the serious situation in the Montreal ports, but a much larger question. The only way collective bargaining can be made to work is by the parties living up to their obligations. It is a system for free people. If they use it to turn their private rights into public wrongs, they drive another coffin nail into this system of free collective bargaining.
I again ask those parties to come to their senses. I ask them not to use the institutions of liberty to destroy their own freedom. Those who will not use the system as it is established by law must take the consequences. The government will not be prepared to frequently intervene on an ad hoc basis to serve the convenience of parties when they willfully set aside their obligations in circumstances that are gravely injurious to the public interest in Canada and to the interests of their community. If we are called upon frequently to do this, then the system of collective bargaining has broken down, and that is a very serious matter indeed, and it will not be enough to call government in to rescue missions. What the parties will find if they wilfully decline to work the collective bargaining system is that a more searching look at the possibility of modification of the overall system will have to be made. In conclusion, I therefore once again call the attention of the parties to this dispute to their obligations.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this motion because it has implications which directly affect all Canada. I shall direct my observations to the manner in which the dispute we are considering will affect the western part of the country. I listened with interest to the minister's speech. It seemed to me, to recall a familiar quotation, that it was full of sound and fury but in the end it signified absolutely nothing. Neither the government nor, in particular, the minister responsible, has had the fortitude to step in to settle this obviously
June 16, 1972

disastrous strike. In these circumstances, I feel compelled to support the motion before us.
Everyone is asking what is the reason for the government's decision not to intervene. In past years, the previous Minister of Labour, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) appeared quite adept at settling or promoting a settlement in disputes of this type. Now, in an election year, it seems to me the Liberals are afraid they might antagonize labour in Quebec and lose their already diminishing support. If a dispute of this kind had occurred in the Port of Vancouver, I feel sure the government would have stepped in long ago and the strike would be well on its way to a resolution. Once again it would seem that political considerations are taking precedence over the more important ones, such as our national economy. Now that the strike has been going on for almost six weeks, and since the union has seen fit to ignore several court injunctions, with the result that grain shipments are being tied up and the economy of Montreal is losing $1 million a day, I think the government should realize that things have gone too far. I would like to know why the minister is hesitant to act.
Mr. Speaker, the first and foremost industry affected by this strike is that of grain exporting. In a recent statement, the Chief Commissioner of the Wheat Board said that the board was frustrated and alarmed at the tie-up in grain shipping. He described the situation as calamitous. Although no sales have yet been lost, it is possible that this strike will lose for Canada possible future sales. The approximate loading capacity of the St. Lawrence system is six million bushels a day. Because longshoremen in Baie Comeau, Sorel and Port Cartier have decided to stay on the job, the St. Lawrence is not shut down completely. Thanks to the extra efforts of the longshoremen in these ports we are able to ship three million bushels a day. But this is hardly sufficient.
However, these delays are not only costing vessel owners millions of dollars, they are harming Canada's image abroad. Our overseas customers must be confident that we are able to meet our commitments and that we stick by our agreements. If we acquire a poor reputation in the grain-buying countries, it will surely affect their decision as to whether they should buy grain from us in future. This would apply to any business contract. There is a concept in contract law called frustration which could discharge parties to an agreement if there were events beyond their control which altered the terms or arrangements of the contract. Mr. Speaker, this does not apply here. In fact, the federal government and the minister have every power to control the situation in Montreal and yet they refuse to act.
The astounding thing about the whole affair is that it is revealed that what is primarily a western Canadian industry can be so radically affected by events in the east with which westerners would otherwise have little concern. Because the health of western agriculture is so vitally dependent on foreign sales, it is clear we must devise a transportation system which is free of impediment and which can funnel the product directly to market. Indeed, in a year when foreign sales have been relatively high, and the government has been loudly proclaiming its own success in that regard, it seems a direct contradiction that
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike the government should allow a situation to develop in which it could lose the very sales it says it has worked so hard to gain for us. What is even more disconcerting is that not only could lack of action on the part of the government affect present sales, if action is not soon taken irreparable harm will be done to our ability to find export markets in the future. Inaction by the present government simply does not make sense. In effect, it is an omission which is sabotaging the efforts of the Wheat Board which is just reaching the point of good salesmanship.
This strike has also shown, along with other events, that our transportation system for exporting grain is in need of revamping. About 60 per cent of the grain destined for overseas goes through the St. Lawrence River terminal elevators and about 35 per cent goes through the west coast. This leaves 5 per cent going through the Port of Churchill. This strike has one useful purpose in that it demonstrates to me that we in the west are entirely too dependent on the port facilities of the St. Lawrence for our own good. Of our export grain shipments, 60 per cent are entirely dependent on this system whose terminal is 1500 miles away from western Canada. Now, it is being demonstrated to us with frightening clarity that a strike or some other unforeseeable political event can devastate our western agricultural industry which is so dependent on foreign sales. I think it is time the federal government started spending more money on the Port of Vancouver. It has been pouring money into the Port of Montreal. Also, it is about time that the government realized the potential of Churchill as a prairie port. The fact that it handles only 5 per cent of export grain when its potential is so much greater is conclusive evidence that the government is favouring eastern interests once again. Mr. Speaker, this strike only proves the necessity of alternative port facilities. Otherwise the west is once again going to suffer because of some event 1500 miles away over which it has no control and for which it has no responsibility.
There are many other aspects of the strike of which I should like to remind the minister and which he certainly did not mention in his speech. I hope that while the minister is pondering his inaction, he realizes the devastating effect that the strike is having on the already depressed economies of Montreal and Quebec City. I imagine that we will hear further about this this afternoon from members associated with those areas.
So far over 135 ships and 425,000 tons of cargo have had to be diverted to other ports. This is costing shipping agents upwards of $100,000 a day and the city of Montreal, which indirectly benefits to the tune of some $200 million in the shipping season, is losing millions of dollars. This is not only a blow to the economy of Montreal, it is also a blow to the economy of Canada. With unemployment in Quebec as high as it is, probably hundreds more have had to be laid off because of the indirect effect of this strike. Apparently the port of Montreal is the largest single economic component in the city, with some 10,000 people depending on it directly for their jobs and many others in service industries also affected.
I sometimes wonder at the logic behind these strikes. From my understanding, it is not only an illegal strike, but

June 16, 1972
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike the reason for it is that management was going to implement a clause to which the union had already agreed. Nevertheless, the union went on strike and even refused arbitration. I should like to know why this particular union should be immune from the law. I am beginning to think that the Quebec provincial Liberals are even exceeded by the federal Liberals in their inability to deal with strikes. I am beginning to think that this union must be more severely dealth with. Although I am not antilabour, I do not agree with pampering unions which do not act reasonably or within the law. By his inaction, this is what the minister is doing.
The minister, as mentioned today, should be prepared to meet directly with the parties involved and spend as much time as necessary with them until a settlement is reached. I know what a Conservative government would do in this situation: we would have the courage to enforce the law if need be. I should like to suggest to the Minister of Labour that he look very seriously at some form of binding arbitration. I think the situation is getting serious enough that this course must be looked at in a realistic light and without any political overtones.
I should like to make reference to an article that appeared in the Montreal Gazette for June 10 dealing with this strike. It quotes the port manager as having said that the loss of the grain trade is the most important effect of the strike. He said that this was the staple upon which the port depended. It seems that everyone is agreed on the disastrous effects of this strike-the port manager, the business community of Montreal, the Wheat Board, the farmers, the shipping agents and the opposition. I suggest that the Liberals join this group and do something about this strike before irreparable harm is done to potential future grain sales as well as to the port of Montreal itself.
One other point in the article that I should like to comment on is the statement that the Wheat Board officials deny there was any definite plan to circumvent the port. I have come to the conclusion that alternative routes for exporting grain will have to be found, and I will not accept any argument to the contrary. In my view, there is no way that we in the west should tolerate this form of strike, or, for that matter, neither should any other area of Canada. Some 3,200 longshoremen hold the present and future prosperity of western Canada in their hands, in effect, by refusing to come to an agreement. If the port of Montreal is going to be subject to irrational union acts such as this which so drastically affect the future of other innocent regions, then I must say that I am in favour of finding ways of circumventing this port and letting the port pick up its losses from grain in some other way when the strike is over.
I have one final point to make. I think that these illegal strikers and the government should realize that they are doing the port of Montreal a disservice by allowing the strike to continue. It can only harm the port and possibly end in a laying off of the longshoremen. The volume of trade is certainly going to be affected for a long period of time, even after the strike is settled. If this is the case, then all I can say is that these strikers and the government will have brought this upon themselves.
In conclusion, I should like to say that we in the west are sick and tired of unions that ignore all reason and go on

strike, tying up the Canadian economy. We are also tired of a government that sits back, does nothing, thus raising many questions about its political conduct.
