subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the longshoremen's strike in Montreal, which has been underway for nearly six weeks, has caused great harm to the port of Montreal and to the general economy in the Montreal area. As a Montreal Member of Parliament, I have said on several occasions that our port is an essential and basic element to the entire Montreal economy. Montreal has gained its prominence in Canada and throughout the world from its importance as a transportation centre. Montreal is the headquarters of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian National Railways, Air Canada, many trucking companies, and it has been the site of the most important port in eastern Canada, a port which feeds into all the other modes of transportation. Montreal has been the gateway for the vast bulk of all our commerce passing between Canada and Europe.
The present longshoremen's strike not only threatens the port of Montreal but has the potential to destroy it as well as a large part of the Montreal economy. It seems to be a suicidal or masochistic exercise on the part of those involved. While it is easy to recognize the damaging aspects of the strike, and the anger and frustration of those who need the port of Montreal to carry on then-business, it is not so easy to find effective solutions. There are no prototype solutions or magic formulae to settle such strikes.
I discussed this on Tuesday evening when I spoke about this matter during the budget debate. What is required is flexibility and discretion. What will work in one case will not work in another. There was great satisfaction in Montreal several months ago when the longshoremen and the Maritime Employers Association signed their new collective agreement-without a strike, by the way-which was praised on all sides as a significant breakthrough in labour relations for port employees. Many persons were forecasting a renaissance for the port which had suffered from continual labour problems in recent years after experiencing a golden age during the 50's and early 60's.
If I understand correctly, the present dispute has arisen in the following way. The collective agreement stipulated that there were to be no changes in work gangs until the fall when the computer dispatch system was to be introduced. Recently, the Maritime Employers Association introduced certain managerial or administrative changes as permitted by the collective agreement. The longshore-
June 16, 1972

men submitted that these were changes in the work gang, but management said they were not. Following this change by management the longshoremen walked out. This was surprising behaviour because the collective agreement signed by the ILA and MEA only a few months ago provided that such disputes on the interpretation of the collective agreement were to be settled by arbitration, and that any party so grieved could have recourse to such arbitration.
In this case, however, the longshoremen disagreed with a move made by management, but they have not made any move to follow the arbitration procedures in the contract. The minister has said that both parties have the right to apply for arbitration, and he is right. It would be highly unusual for management to request arbitration on their own actions, that is on a change which they consider to be legal and which they introduced under the collective agreement. Furthermore, the longshoremen have stated they will not go to arbitration and they will not recognize arbitration in this manner. This means that if management went to arbitration on their own, they would not only be appealing their own actions but would be involved in ex parte arbitration, running the risk that the arbitration board might rule against them, while on the other hand, even if they should win they would gain nothing. The longshoremen stated they would not recognize the ruling, consequently can the Maritime Employers Association be blamed for not going to arbitration by themselves? The Maritime Employers Association has said it would be willing to go to arbitration with the longshoremen and that it would recognize the arbitration ruling whether it won or lost.
This is an illegal strike and, with all due respect for the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Osier), it is not a lockout. I have not heard anybody claim it to be a lockout until this point.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I am sure this is said in error, that I termed it a lockout or something. I do not recall having said anything about this strike today, yesterday or any day in the immediate past.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
I apologize to the hon. member. I was referring to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that this is an illegal strike and we should ask what can be done. In the first instance, the Maritime Employers Association or the government could prosecute the union and union leaders under the provisions of the Canada Labour Code, but it is questionable whether this would be the best means of settling this dispute at this time. This action could be taken under Sections 128, 147 and 152 of the Canada Labour Code, Revised Statutes of Canada 1970. The government could intervene either by putting the port and union under trusteeship, or by imposing compulsory arbitration on its own. This could be done either under the labour code or by special law, and I will discuss this in greater detail.
Section 159 of the Canada Labour Code, which was Section 56 in the former Revised Statutes, reads:
The Minister may either upon application or of his own initiative, where he deems it expedient, make or cause to be made any inquiries he thinks fit regarding industrial matters-
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
I am not referring to that part, but it continues:
-and may do such things as seem calculated to maintain or secure industrial peace and to promote conditions favourable to settlement of disputes.
That section sets out the ways in which this could be done, and suggests certain action that can be taken. The government has intervened in this manner in the past, and also through legislation. It has always reserved the right to do so when the public interest requires it. The manner in which this action is taken, however, is extremely important. If the government announces immediately that it will intervene if a settlement is not reached by a certain deadline, then all pressure is taken off the parties to reach a settlement themselves.
Furthermore, in a case like this, if the government had intervened immediately it would not have helped the longterm interest of collective bargaining or freely arrived at collective agreements. This was pointed out by the minister. What value would there be in negotiating a collective agreement, including an arbitration provision, if one of the parties could disregard its own signed agreement and have the government intervene to impose a settlement or a new type of arbitration? If this became a precedent, collective bargaining would become useless. That having been said, there is a time for the government to intervene, but such an intervention should not be a precedent; nor should it be announced in advance. This type of action must be taken with great discretion and wisdom.
During the last few years we have had two important commissions on labour relations. One was the Woods Commission appointed by the Pearson government in 1968, and the other was the recent Cohen Commission in Newfoundland. The report of the latter commission was tabled recently by the Newfoundland government. Let me refer to some of the things the Woods Commission says about public interest and essential service disputes. The report makes seven observations. It is extremely difficult to say in advance in what industries a strike or lockout should be curtailed. The length of a strike or lockout is a critical factor. There is no one policy that can work with uniform success. Flexibility of approach is essential. The determination that a given stoppage of work should be terminated in the public interest is a political decision. This political element is an inducement to the parties to drive the dispute beyond any procedural device and into the political arena. Circumstances may be expected to arise in the course of the industrial conflict in which the fear of the law will be not so strong it will forestall the breaking of that law.
The Woods Commission recommended a three man public interest disputes commission. It recommended that this commission have two functions; first, to determine special procedures for resolving disputes in industries under federal jurisdiction which are prone to disputes that jeopardize the public interest. These procedures might include non-binding arbitration and voluntary binding arbitration as well as the involvement of the commission itself. In the handling of actual disputes by this commission, in which the public interest is threatened, the government should be able to request from the commission a report recommending procedures to terminate the dispute, including possible seizure, trusteeship, partial

June 16, 1972
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
arbitration of a statutory strike or compulsory arbitration. This could be implemented by act of Parliament.
I,	personally, feel that when the strike begins to seriously affect the public interest, then the government must intervene. I have come to the conclusion that this should have been done as of yesterday, and I said so publicly at that time. I feel that the government should order that the men be returned to work and that all outstanding issues be referred to arbitration. If it is necessary, this should be done by special legislation. The minister has said he would not want to do anything to undermine the collective agreement or the collective bargaining process. Generally, I would agree with him, but in this case at this time I believe the collective agreement has been undermined, if not completely destroyed.
The minister has stated that there are arbitration provisions in the collective agreement. He once again appealed to both sides to use them. It seems to me the time has come when we cannot leave this question to the private decision of management and labour alone. I must remind the House once again of some of the things I said last Tuesday evening. Labour relations are such today that there is not only a management and labour interest but also a public interest. In many cases a long, serious strike hurts the public interest much more than it does management or labour.

speechtext: You said that the other day.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
Yes. I am repeating it because it is important. I should like to quote some of the things I said on Tuesday evening. As reported in Hansard at page 3104, I said:
The basis of the right to strike, which is that the cost to both union and to management will eventually force both to arrive at a compromise, I submit is no longer valid since, first of all, the cost of many strikes is now borne by the public, particularly in the service industries such as transport, education, garbage removal and so on. Second, in other cases the cost of a strike is carried by suppliers and sellers of a product.
I gave the example of a recent canning strike which ruined many tomato growers while only partially inconveniencing union and management. There was hardly any cost to management and labour but the tomato growers were completely ruined by the strike. I referred to agreements arrived at recently in certain countries where the employees of one airline were on strike. It was agreed that the additional revenue gained by other airlines would, after deduction of costs, be given to the struck airline, or management simply could raise prices.
I conclude by again referring to a quotation. I do so because it is important. I wish to repeat the quotation I gave in the House the other night and to which many people have recently referred. Mr. George Meany, head of the AF of L-CIO, stated recently that labour should voluntarily replace strikes with reliance upon binding arbitration for a one-year period. He said that the strike is a nineteenth century tactic, and with the advent of corporate giants and correspondingly super-unions, strikes become even-matched struggles which drag on for weeks,

radiating economic shock waves far beyond the limits of the actual conflict.
I cannot understand the minister when he says that government intervention at this time would destroy the collective agreement or destroy the collective bargaining process, because we have intervened in this way in the past. In this case the parties to some extent have already destroyed the collective agreement. It seems ludicrous to me that as Montreal goes down the drain, the government, which is to protect the public interest, clings to principles which have already been thrown out by those whom they are meant to serve.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade), has conscientiously and seriously presented a motion calling on the government to immediately end the dock strike. As a member for the Montreal area of Lachine, Dorval and Ste. Claire I am proud to have seconded the motion. It is too bad that just at the end of the speech of the hon. member for Sainte-Marie, the hon. member for Temis-camingue (Mr. Caouette) refused to allow the hon. member to finish his speech, because there were important proposals the hon. member wished to make. As the seconder of his motion, I want at the outset to read into the record his proposals, if you do not mind, Mr. Speaker.

The solutions proposed by the hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade) are as follows:
The Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) should:
A)	call the bargaining agents who have participated in the preparation of the agreement for both parties and invite them to convince their respective groups to use arbitration;
B)	make a specific statement in which he should establish the disastrous effects of this impasse on our economy and indicate clearly that in the public interest the situation could not last longer;
C)	advise the parties that if they do not start arbitration procedures pursuant to their agreement within 48 hours, the minister will appoint one of the arbitrators designated in the agreement;
D)	implement section 5-01 (7) concerning grievances;
E)	immediately express his intention to amend the Canada Labour Code so that the Department of Labour could intervene immediately by imposing arbitration when the parties refuse to do so;
F)	provide for a procedure ensuring that in any labour-management dispute under his jurisdiction, the federal government will see to it that a secret ballot is compulsory in labour union meetings and reflects a minimum membership participation for a work stoppage or strike to be decided.

It is too bad the hon. member for Temiscamingue did not give the hon. member permission to put forward these proposals at the end of his speech. I think this was stupidity on his part.
The Quebec illegal, wildcat dock strike is the worst strike in Quebec's history. In economic terms, its effects will be very harmful to Montreal for years to come. In fact, there will be no catching up; what is lost will remain lost. The $200 million yearly input into the Montreal economy is being dwindled away, and 10,000 jobs are directly affected. An equal number of persons are indirectly affected. Alternative shipping routes have been found. As a result of these alternative shipping routes
June 16, 1972

having been established, the shipping that has been lost may not return to Montreal.
The transportation hub of Montreal is threatened to such an extent that this loss may be permanent. One hundred and thirty-two ships left Montreal with full holds or were diverted to other ports at the beginning of the strike. Prairie grain is being shipped by alternate routes. There is talk of flour mills moving their operations out of our province. This would result in loss of jobs, pensions, and so on.
Management has appealed to the federal government to take action to stop the strike. The Montreal Chamber of Commerce has asked that the federal government take action. The only action taken so far by the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) is indicated in a release from his department entitled "Labour News Headlines", issued by the Canada Department of Labour on June 2, which reads:
Labour minister, Martin O'Connell, has refused to permit St. Lawrence stevedoring firms to prosecute a union of 3,250 dock-workers on strike for more than three weeks in defiance of court injunctions.
The government is shirking its responsibility in this illegal, wildcat strike. As always in situations such as this, the government has taken a laissez faire attitude. Like an ostrich, it has hidden its head in the sand and hopes that the problems will disappear by themselves. This government has allowed the deterioration of port business in the Montreal area to take place. This has affected 10,000 jobs directly and another 10,000 related jobs.
In other words, this government has again capitulated, as it has in the case of every strike affecting the federal jurisdiction. It capitulated in other dock strikes. It capitulated when our airports were shut down. It capitulated in the seaway workers' strike. It has often capitulated by allowing things to happen and never taking the initiative. This government is so weak that it has lost its credibility. It should not remain in office. This government has allowed the U.S.S.R. to build turbines for Canada, to the detriment of Dominion Engineering Works in Lachine and of Canadian expertise. It has allowed the importation of huge generators and transformers, to the detriment of Canadian manufacturers and Canadian expertise. It has allowed the importation of machinery for the production of paper, to the detriment of Canadian manufacturers and Canadian expertise.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have attempted to give examples of how this government has allowed things to happen which are detrimental to the economy of our country. I am referring to strikes and other situations in which the government has taken no action. Since 1968 this government has capitulated whenever a strike has taken place. It has allowed our economy to deteriorate by adding more unemployment to the unemployment already caused by its policy to fight inflation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has publicly confessed to this policy on many occasions.
This strike is now in its sixth week, and the government continues to refuse to intervene. It has failed to put an end to the strike. It has capitulated at every turn. This government does not lead, nor is it led. It has lost its credibility, and in fact it has no moral right to remain in office after June of next year.

speechtext:
Quite frankly, as a farmer I myself can get the grain to market. If the hon. member can tell me, when he makes his speech, how I can get the grain past the port of Montreal, the port of Vancouver, or somewhere else, directly to the customer I would be only too happy to hear how it can be done. I like to think that people who work at these ports recognize that they have a product to handle and it is important to people such as

June 16, 1972
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike myself, representing a farm community which grows a product, to have it shipped to the customer. We live in an interdependent world. The matter before us points this up more than anything else.
I would be cautious about laying the blame on either management or labour in this respect. I am not close to the situation and therefore I am not in a position to judge. But I do stress the importance of this problem not only to the city of Montreal, the city of Quebec, the province of Quebec or the businessmen there, but to the economy as a whole, particularly to the people of Saskatchewan, the province from which I come.
As I listened earlier to the minister speaking about the problem, I was reminded of the story of the businessman who was travelling on a train. He went into the diner and ordered a particular pudding for dessert. For some reason this pudding was not available. The businessman became very angry and said, "My company gives this railroad hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of business every year, yet when I get on this train you cannot even supply me with a dish of pudding". The chef happened to know that they were coming to a large city and he wired ahead to have the pudding ready when the train arrived there. Just as the train was pulling into the station it was time for dessert, and they rushed a dish of pudding to the businessman and offered it to him. But the businessman would not eat it. He said, "I would rather be mad".
When I listened to the minister refer to these two parties not even wanting to come to the bargaining table, I was reminded of the story. They would rather be mad at each other than get together and solve the problem. I suggest that perhaps the two parties concerned should look at the situation in that light. I would say to them: Grow up a little.
We in the Prairies have known for some time that we must ship much of our grain to markets outside of Canada through the St. Lawrence Seaway, and in this case much of it goes through Montreal. This just goes to show that if someone sneezes in Montreal, someone on the Prairies is apt to catch a cold. If there is no sale or movement of grain on the Prairies, this is soon reflected in the industry of Ontario and Quebec. It all demonstrates how interdependent we are in this age.
This points to the need to develop new measures to solve industrial disputes. I ask you to notice, Mr. Speaker, that I do not say labour disputes. They are industrial disputes because there are two sides to them. As I say, we have to evolve new methods for solving them. I have some ideas but I hesitate to suggest them in an emergency situation that has given rise to an atmosphere where anger and hard feelings have been shown. But we can point to other countries where workers do not go on strike over every little problem that develops. Here I think of Sweden especially.
As a Saskatchewan farmer, I emphasize the importance of sales of grain to export markets. At the moment these sales are quite large. But it is not enough that we sell the grain, we must also get it to market and, logically, much of it must go through the port of Montreal and the St. Lawrence Seaway. While the price we get for our grain

may not be as attractive as farmers would like, the large volume of sales has somewhat alleviated their problems. As a result, it is necessary that we keep a large volume of grain moving. Much of it must go through the St. Lawrence Seaway.
The problem is not confined to this year alone. If we have an unfavourable labour record at Montreal it will jeopardize our sales in succeeding years. Customers wonder about our ability to move grain. A similar situation arose recently in the port of New York. There were many problems at that port, many industrial disputes, as a result of which businessmen started to arrange to transfer their business elsewhere over a long period of time.
As a grain shipper from western Canada, I would like to point out to hon. members who represent the city of Montreal that western farmers are concerned about the reputation of the port of Montreal. If we cannot ship our grain through Montreal we will have to take a closer look at developing the port of Churchill, at enlarging facilities at Prince Rupert and placing better facilities at Vancouver. But logically Montreal is one port through which we should be shipping grain. Let me simply say that if the problem continues we will have to look elsewhere. This is a problem that affects not only Montreal but the people of the Prairies.
The National Farmers Union has suggested that, if necessary, the government might take over the port facilities at Montreal until the present problem is resolved. I suggest that the Department of Labour should be looking at this matter quite closely if the strike cannot be resolved by some other means. I heard the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) argue with a great deal of eloquence about the way strikes are settled in this day and age. But, Mr. Speaker, this strike is not being settled. I think the minister might use his moral authority a little more forcefully. Sometimes in a situation of this kind the moral leadership given by a minister can bring the parties together and make them ashamed of themselves for not negotiating. It is not enough for the minister to sit in Ottawa and scold them from a distance; he should show a little more initiative and leadership directly on the spot, in the hope that this might resolve the situation.
One hon. member from Montreal has reported on the effect of the dispute on business in that city. This reminds me of a friend who once told me that it is a poor business deal that does not benefit both parties. Mr. Speaker, in this case the public is the third party and it is a poor deal for all parties when there is no settlement of the strike. I wish to make just one more point. I recall working one winter on the railway in the city of Toronto. I came from the Prairies, where everyone is known and, indeed, where everyone is important. There is no problem there about identification. But I came into a big city and began working for a big railroad. The workers were represented by a big union and I can recall wondering about the problem of self-identification. I may have felt quite important back home, but nobody seemed to care in Toronto. If some day a man didn't show up for work, they just got somebody else to take his place.
I cannot help feeling that part of the problem connected with the settlement of disputes is that nobody knows, nobody cares. Whether you go to work or do not go to
June 16, 1972

work is not noticed, unless there is a strike. Sometimes the only reward or attention you get is when you do something out of the way. This is part of the total problem. This sense of identification, of being needed and wanted, must be examined in a society where cities are growing larger, where businesses are becoming bigger and where labour is represented by larger organizations. If this problem is tackled, some of the other problems may be easier to resolve.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me to rise and discuss the question raised this morning by the hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade).
The hon. member dealt with the question of the port of Montreal and said it was urgent to move a motion to this effect. However, it is unfortunate that himself and the hon. member for Lachine (Mr. Rock), who just resumed his seat, turned the serious problem of the strike in Quebec ports into a political issue.
Speakers from the two other parties have dealt sensible with this problem and proposed to the minister and the government various ways of settling it. But they did not try to turn it into a political issue which, I suggest, would have been quite out of place. There is an appropriate time for everything. Some issues may be used for politicking but I think that this problem is so serious that we should refrain from petty politics as has been attempted today.
I might go as far as agreeing that this motion had become necessary, even though I do not fully endorse it, because it must be kept in mind that even though this motion comes from the opposition, there are Montreal members on this side of the House. And even if, day after day, we do not put any questions to the minister in this connection, this does not mean that we are not concerned. In fact, as a member from Montreal, I can state along with my colleagues from that area that we have discussed this matter many times with the minister and that we are quite anxious to find a solution to this problem which threatens to get worse every day.
If the government tries to settle a public problem too hastily, it is told: You have not given the union and union members enough time to settle their problems with their employers. If the government postpones its intervention and gives more freedom to the union and union members for further discussion with employers, it is told: You are too slow to act.
In fact, I can affirm that my colleagues from the Montreal area, as well as myself, have often discussed this matter with the minister. We are quite willing to find a solution to the problem which might get worse as the days go by.
True, as I said a while ago, we are aware of the prejudice caused by this dispute to the economy of Montreal and the area. It is estimated at $1 million per day. Since the goods cannot be unloaded in the port of Montreal, they must be routed to Toronto, Halifax or elsewhere, which, besides causing a direct loss to the port of Montreal, results also in losses for the Montreal area carriers who used to provide that service.
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
Some goods are held in other ports, so that dealers run the risk of losing sales. Extra storage, trucking and freight charges add to the cost of such goods, which is prejudicial to the economy and explains why this problem has become quite serious. And this is why we have had extensive public discussions with the minister and some of his officials.
When the collective agreement between the Longshoremen's or "Stevedores" Union-as they like to be called- and the Maritime Employers Association of Montreal harbour was signed last March, it was hailed by both parties as the best agreement in North America. Everyone gloried in the fact that for the first time in years peace might have returned to Quebec harbours which could thus resume their former place in Canada. Actually, it must be recognized that for the last four or five years, the situation in Quebec harbours, particularly in Montreal, has not been an easy one. And following the signing of this collective agreement which gave Canadian longshoremen greater benefits than American stevedores enjoy, people thought that the situation had been settled and that within the next two or three years, Montreal harbour would thrive once again, that jobs would be created and, by the same token, that the whole metropolitan area would reap these benefits. Unfortunately, this agreement was short-lived.
As a solution, it was suggested that an inquiry commission be established. As the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) has indicated, the establishment of an inquiry commission would delay the solution of the problem. Too much time would elapse before the chairman of this commission could be selected, before hearing the evidence of those who favour or oppose the establishment of the commission, and before being acquainted with the views of both parties, in order to reach a decision.
Today, I am of the opinion that the minister has waited for the parties to come to an agreement, but they do not want to. The matter is becoming more urgent day by day.
The hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade) read into the record this morning the French version of the collective agreement dealing with grievances, but I must now quote from the English text since it is the only copy at hand. Subsection D) of Section 5 of the Grievance Procedure is very clear, and I quote:
(d) A request for arbitration may be initiated by either the union or the Maritime Employers Association. The party requesting the arbitrator shall set forth in writing the matter submitted to the arbitrator and send a copy of it to the other party.

Today, Mr. Speaker, the employers' syndicate says: We are quite willing to go to arbitration, but the International Longshoremen Association does not agree. The longshoremen union says: "We refuse, and we are right to do it."
Nor do we, the Minister and I, want to act as arbitrators. Nor does the government. In view of the fact that this collective agreement was freely entered into by both parties and since it is provided in this section that either party may ask to go to arbitration, the dispute can only be settled now if the longshoremen union or the employer's

June 16, 1972
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
Association applies for arbitration. If either party can apply for it and if the appeal can be heard as provided in the collective agreement, I call on the more intelligent of the two parties, to take such action.
Let neither of the two say: I do not want to do it because the other party does not want to. Is either of them afraid of the arbitrators' decision?
This collective agreement also supplies the name of four persons who could be chosen as arbitrators to settle a grievance. And I know from good authority that the first name on this list is the hon. Mr. Justice A. B. Gold, who is ready and available for hearing this dispute. But if the judge wishes to hear the grievances, they must be presented.
That reminds me of a small family quarrel, when husband and wife through pride or conceit do not want to give in.
It is necessary in the public interest, in that of the Canadian economy and particularly in that of Quebec which suffers so much from all those conflicts between unions and management, to come to an agreement.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to say here that employers are wrong or blame the longshoremen's union. It will be for the judge to find the solution to the problem.
The few notes which I have on the collective agreement are very simple and very clear. Section 5 (g) reads as follows:

(g)	The arbitrator will have jurisdiction over any question relating to the interpretation or application of this agreement as well as the application modalities and implementation of an arbitration decision, but he will in no case be empowered to amend, add to, or delete any part of this agreement.
(h)	The arbitrator's decision will be final and binding.

Mr. Speaker, that is clear and simple. If the two parties involved do not step forward and ask for arbitration-and I trust the Minister of Labour-the two parties will have to sit at the same table and a final decision will have to be reached.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that both parties know, the longshoremen's union as well as the employers' association, that sooner or later solutions will be applied. I wonder, however-because I know they are intelligent men-whether after five weeks of delay that have forced 150 ships to sail to other Canadian ports, it might not be time for the parties involved to ask for arbitration themselves.
This is only a plea. I do not accuse one party or the other. I would not want to be the judge who will decide, but the collective agreement is quite clear. I am not a lawyer, but it is so clear and simple that I have easily understood that the parties have all the powers, but they will have to put their pride or self-respect aside and refer their problem to the judge, so that he may consider it, in order to find a solution.
We must keep in mind that the economy of Quebec is affected by that conflict, as I said a while ago. It is losing $1 million daily.

Mr. Speaker, I ask again the employers' organization as well as the longshoremen's union to resort to arbitration.
So far, questions have been put to the minister in the House, and he has repeated, day after day-and I would have said the same thing-that he dared not get involved in a collective agreement which, as I said earlier, has been signed in good faith by both parties, an agreement in which the use of computers is dealt with.
The hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) said this morning that computers were already installed. If my information is accurate, they are not, but will be only in September, and there seems to be some disagreement, now, regarding this. If I remember correctly-I do not have the text of the agreement before me-as long as the computers are not working, the clauses of the old agreement will apply.
It seems that following the one-day walkout, out of sympathy for the labour common front about the troubles which occurred recently in the province of Quebec, the Maritime Employers' Association has changed its position and said that this one-day strike was a breach of contract. It may be true because such a day was not provided in the contract and there was a breach of contract.
I think this was unfortunate and I appeal to altruism because there is no doubt employers are never affected by a strike; it is the employees who suffer. Unions always manage rather well, but the employees get hurt.
I was talking yesterday to one of the Montreal blue collars who have just ended a 5-week strike and I jokingly welcomed him and his truck to the Montreal area. He pointed out to me that before the strike he was eating in a restaurant but since he was not working he ate sandwiches.
I will spare the House the language he used as it would not be parliamentary. I mean to say that the same thing happens each time there is a strike.
I received between 1 and 2 o'clock a group of young students from my constituency who attended part of the debate. They asked a few questions about its nature and its effects. And I was pleased to tell them what it was all about.
There is a solution which other hon. members have mentioned, and I believe, it is getting increasingly imperative to come to it in labour-management relations. More than ever before, I think, it is time to establish in all fields of endeavour-and I spoke to the Minister of Labour about it-a council or a supreme labour tribunal, because on many occasions strikes are settled only after 5, 6 or 7 weeks and often the employers' proposals made in the beginning of the negotiation period are accepted. The pattern is always the same: it is always the small man who suffers.
I live in a labour district where strikes are frequent, and those who are the most needy are always the ones who suffer the most, and not union leaders nor management, because these have always the means to wait and to recoup. And management often brings pressure to bear against unions.
June 16, 1972

It is time to start establishing fair and effective standards and making available to employees all the means and resources required to air their grievances. I am generally in favour of labour unions, although in some cases I may have reservations about their integrity.
About a year ago, I made a speech in which I was condemning the unions on a specific matter. As a general rule unions have a right to exist, but there are still too many workers who are not unionized, unfortunately.
We may hope that in the present conflict union members will land on their feet and those aware of the terms of the longshoremen's collective agreement know that their remuneration is quite high. However, they themselves will be penalized and the consequences will affect the economy.
I therefore renew my request, appealing as sympathetically, as humanely as possible to both the Employers Association and the Longshoremen's union, that one of the other party call for arbitration. The collective agreement, I repeat, was signed in good faith, both parties agreeing to the paragraph I mentioned providing that if either party files such a request for arbitration the mediator will have to hear the case and render a decision, since something must be done, and otherwise the government will eventually have to take action.
If the Maritime employers' Association or the International Longshoremen's Association do not fill out a request by this weekend, I shall urge the minister of Labour to intervene early next week.
I understand his reluctance to get involved in an agreement that was concluded between these parties, but if neither of them, as prescribed by the collective agreement, files a request for arbitration, I would ask the Minister of Labour to intervene at the very beginning of next week so that a solution to the problem of Quebec ports may be found.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
It goes without saying that when we have before the House an issue such as we have today, as a western member vitally interested in the transportation of grain to market I should rise in my place and comment on this very serious situation.
First, Mr. Speaker, I wish to compliment the hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade) for bringing forward the important matter of the Montreal dockworkers' strike through his motion under our rules which allow
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
opposition members to raise matters of great urgency. I also compliment the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) and the hon. member for Lachine (Mr. Rock) for their very comprehensive remarks in connection with this serious matter.
I should like to review some of the events leading to the present serious situation. I trust hon. members will excuse me if I take up the time of the House for a few minutes; I was not here during all the speeches made this afternoon. In any event, I believe the people of Saskatchewan will be interested in the preliminary observations I have to make in connection with the great port of Montreal and the effect the strike there will have on the Canadian economy generally as well as upon Montreal itself.
I should like to list a few of these events. National Harbours Board ports in Canada handled a record 93.7 million tons of traffic in 1971, up by 7.9 per cent from 1970. The port of Montreal, however, showed a decline of
5.4	per cent in tonnage handled during the same period. Since May 16 the port of Montreal has been paralyzed by striking longshoremen numbering about 3,200. The ports of Quebec and Trois-Rivieres are also affected. Grain is the staple item of commerce on which the ports depend, and since the strike began 500,000 tons of grain have been diverted to other ports.
According to the chairman of the Wheat Board, Canada will be unable to honour her commitments in respect of European markets because of the strike. I shall repeat that statement because it is of vital interest to myself personally, to my province and, I am sure, to all of western Canada. According to the chairman of the Wheat Board, Canada will be unable to honour her commitments respecting wheat shipments to European markets, as planned, because of the strike.
I should like to give the House some background information with respect to this strike which is paralyzing the great harbour of Montreal. It is costing shipping agents in Montreal alone an estimated $100,000 a day. The cost to the community in lost salaries and direct income exceeds $1 million a day. At least 132 ships have sailed from Montreal or have been diverted from the port with full holds. This represents a loss of 425,000 tons of cargo. Ten thousand people depend directly on the port for jobs, and many times this number employed in service industries are adversely affected by the strike.
The port pumps approximately $250 million a year into the Montreal economy. A consortium of five large Japanese shipping companies which has been scouting for an eastern Canadian terminus for its ships has decided to give Montreal a wide berth even as a secondary distribution centre. A foreign automobile manufacturer who had been seriously considering Montreal as a base for increased unloading capacity in eastern Canada, is having second thoughts. Material for a display destined for China and vaunting the strength of the Canadian economy is held up in the strikebound port. Export grains shipments to Russia and other destinations across the Atlantic have been rescheduled out of terminals on the north shore of the St. Lawrence River and more than 100 jobs in the Montreal area could disappear as a result.

June 16, 1972
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
Mr. Speaker, I believe hon. members would be interested in a further brief outline of the main events in this dispute. On March 30 of this year management and labour signed a three-year contract aimed at improving the port's obviously low productivity by eliminating the outmoded gang system. In return, the employers provided the men with job security and a lucrative pension scheme. The agreement was subsequently ratified by the union rank and file. Irregular work stoppages began on May 9, culminating in a walkout by 3,200 longshoremen on May 16. The strike directly affects the harbours of Montreal, Quebec and Trois-Rivieres, paralyzing transport over much of eastern Canada.
What was the main cause of this strike? The main gripe which set off the wildcat action arose from dissatisfaction over changes made in the system of work gangs. In the last labour contract management won the right to break up the work gangs. They were to be replaced by a computer system which was to come into effect this fall. Instead of a constant unit of 17 men doing all jobs, the computer would call up only those men needed for any particular task. The men signed and ratified the agreement, but when the break-up of the work gangs started, they walked out.
What was the reaction of management to this situation? Attempts at negotiation failed and three court injunctions ordering the men back to work were ignored. On May 31, the Maritime Employers Association suspended the striking longshoremen. Management has offered to ask for arbitration providing the union will attend the sessions and abide by the decision of an independent arbitrator. As yet there has been no success in bringing the two parties together. Labour took the following position: the day after their suspension, about 300 members of Montreal local 375 of the ILA voted to continue the walkout at the three St. Lawrence ports. Only about one-tenth of the available union members took part in the vote. The union president said the men were prepared to stay out for as long as was necessary to gain a satisfactory settlement. An unnamed spokesman for the union stated there was no question of arbitration.
The federal government took its usual position in such cases. The Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) has repeatedly called on either or both parties to make use of the arbitration clause in their contract in order to settle the dispute. He has often declared his intention not to interfere, both to this House and to the press. It is the usual story-Nero fiddled while Rome burned.
Let us review, now, the short-term problems resulting from this strike. Until the early 1960s the port of Montreal enjoyed an enviable reputation. It could handle goods more cheaply than anywhere else in North America. Labour relations, though paternalistic, were good and strikes were infrequent. In the late 1960s, government and labour forces pushed through a contract on behalf of the International Longshoremen's Association which, among other things, fixed the size of labour gangs unloading ships at an arbitrary number regardless of the number actually needed. Production declined drastically. One Montreal company estimates that in 1966, 20-man gangs handled about 35 tons of flour an hour. Today, 17-man gangs handle a maximum of 16 tons an hour. This means

ships stay in port for longer periods at a cost of between $2,500 and $3,000 a day. This has grave implications for the future of the port since an important factor in the scheduling of shipping today is the speed at which cargo can be unloaded.
Statistics Canada reports that more vessles visited Montreal in 1971 than in 1970, and figures issued by the National Harbours Board shows steady increases in general cargo tonnage handled over the past five years. Nevertheless, the effects of United States dock strikes on certain Canadian ports may have inflated the figures in relation to the total cargo handled. In fact, Montreal's through cargo declined by 5.4 per cent in 1971.
Canadian Pacific, although its headquarters is in Montreal, located its new container terminal in Quebec City, claiming it was more economic. And last summer a gang of shippers suggested that one solution to Montreal's labour problems would be to close the port. "Most of us can do our shipping through maritime ports with only minor inconvenience or additional cost; it is drastic but it might be the only way," said one company president.
Federal intervention has done little to ease the problems plaguing the labour situation. In the recent Montreal longshoremen's strike federal intervention has been non-existent. Despite pleas by the Montreal Chamber of Commerce and the Quebec Truckers Association, the Minister of Labour has refused to interfere. Rather, he has repeatedly called for either or both parties to make use of an arbitration clause in their contract to settle the dispute. Federal failure is not limited to labour relations. Its transportation policy, as it applies specifically to Montreal and generally to all ports under the National Harbours Board, has failed adequately to assess the needs of and directions for the future administration of the port.
A year ago, on May 12, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) announced a new policy for ports. He proposed creation of local port authorities for each of the nine major ports now administered by the National Harbours Board. These local port authorities were to be representative of all local interests including management and labour, municipal and provincial authorities. Each was to have a good deal of authority, including consultation in the appointment of port managers, the preparation of budgets, forward planning and other important matters. At that time the Minister of Transport stated that the federal objective "must be concerned with the good of all Canadians and not just with any particular vested interest".
However, various comments by those asked to serve on the local port authorities raise serious questions about the eventual success of the federal government's objectives. In Montreal, several men asked to serve and the port authorities flatly refused. They pointed out that they could not very well run a major enterprise which would require them to make decisions regarding their own competitors. There could be also a conflict of interest with labour appointees in a decision between the efficient running of the harbour concerned and the demands of the labour union members. Conflicts of interest could well cause serious damage to the harbour concerned. Instead
June 16, 1972

of serving national interests, the port authorities could easily become involved in individual concerns, reflecting the make-up of the local boards.
What is therefore needed, and what has not yet been suggested by the Minister of Transport-despite the fact that members of the port authorities of Montreal, Halifax, St. John's, Saint John, Quebec, Trois-Rivieres, Churchill, Manitoba and Vancouver have been announced-is government controls. The Minister of Transport must place controls on the power of the National Ports Council's influence over the Department of Transport and the National Harbours Board. He must also establish who is going to be responsible for policy-making and for coordinating the activities of the various ports. These controls are essential if the outcome is to be fair to all concerned in all regions of the country.
What is the long term prospect, Mr. Speaker? A major problem affecting Montreal in the long run, as in the short run, is its lack of effective administration. The newly established port authority in its present form does not promise much improvement over the past administrative performance of the National Harbours Board. And yet the future of Montreal's harbour depends upon adequate planning and definition of goals. Further, it is important that the establishment of these goals be made in the context of nationwide transport policy which realistically reflects the potential of Montreal within an integrated national system.
The future of shipping lies in containerization. A critical factor in profitable and efficient ocean container transportation is to see that inland container movement and inland terminals adapt to increasing flows. According to R. R. Cope, vice-president of research for the Department of Transport:
The critical factor in influencing the directional flow of containerized cargo between the Atlantic hinterland and overseas points through the Atlantic and St. Lawrence ports will likely be the adjustments made by the inland carriers in rates and services to accommodate containerization.
In the context of substantial increases in container traffic, Montreal's future is not good. The port's potential is limited by its spatial placement between the river and railway tracks. There is little room, and no plans for future expansion to permit quick unloading of large quantities of containerized cargo. As well, the proximity of the harbour to the downtown centre hinders quick and easy access to and from the waterfront both by trains and/or trucks. Essential to efficient sea-land transport is the facility of access for loaded vehicles to main trucking and train routes.
Obviously, the direction of future development for the harbour of Montreal must be studied carefully. It is most important that the port's potential be seen in the context of national goals. If an east coast port, such as Halifax, can be more suitably developed as the main container terminal for eastern Canada, then futile dreams of maintaining Montreal as the country's premier general cargo port must die. The port's future role must be assessed according to its potential but, as has been stressed, in the context of future directions of transportation methods as they affect the entire country.
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
Bringing this matter closer to home rather than speaking in general terms about how it affects the entire country, I ask, how does it affect our agricultural industry? It affects it in a most serious way, particularly my province of Saskatchewan which produces so much grain and depends on our major ports to keep this grain moving to world markets. Our party, on checking only yesterday with officials of the Canadian Wheat Board, found that the board, as well as all other representatives of the Canadian grain trade and farm organizations, are expressing the greatest alarm at the cutback in grain shipments from the port of Montreal. The government cannot salve its conscience by saying the grain will move through other ports. The fact is that these ports are now working to capacity in most cases and can not be expected to handle the extra volume of large amounts of grain. This means delayed deliveries to our customers, possible loss of markets to certain customers and a direct drop in farmers' income.
The fact is that the only remaining hope that even our large grain producers in the west have is that they produce large yields per acre and market these yields on a larger quota annually, having regard to the much lower price per bushel our farmers are now receiving for all their grain products. I want to re-emphasize what the hon. member for Lisgar referred to in his speech a few minutes ago, and that is that the effect of the Montreal dockwork-ers' strike more than points up the fact that the government should immediately take steps to enlarge grain handling facilities at both the ports of Churchill and Vancouver.
