speakeroldname: Mr. Ian Watson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member from the Montreal area and representative of a riding through which the St. Lawrence Seaway passes, I am very much interested in the prosperity of the port of Montreal, as are also several of my fellow-citizens from the south shore area of Montreal.

A number of factors with which we are all too familiar have combined during the past few years to put, if not the future at least the future greatness of Montreal in doubt. Located at the entrance to the Great Lakes industrial heartland of North America, surrounded by the richest agricultural land in Quebec, within easy distance of abundant mineral resources, and endowed with one of the world's most scenic locations, Montreal attracts an energetic and cosmopolitan population which gives to this city an incomparable spirit and character. Being so richly endowed with human and physical resources, I am convinced that Montreal's future is to be to Canada what New York is to the United States. Yet if that is Montreal's objective, we have lost ground.
Never before has it been more important to fight against the narrow-mindedness which, if it were success-

June 16, 1972
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike ful, would make Montreal a city of strictly regional or provincial importance. The authorities in Montreal and Quebec, as well as the federal member from Quebec, must give strong support to broadening Montreal's national and international role. One essential element of Montreal's future depends directly on the federal government, and that is our port: it stands closed today almost forsaken by all maritime transport companies.

The strike now in progress, unexpected as it was in the midst of the general euphoria surrounding the signing of the three-year contract, is a terrible setback not only to Montreal's legitimate aspirations to greatness in maritime commerce but to the entire business atmosphere of this great city. The side effects of port activity on Montreal business are enormous. This port brings in revenue from customs and excise duties, not necessarily all attributable to maritime activity, of $329 million a year. In addition, the money generated by port activities is a figure somewhere around $225 million. I think that is probably a low figure.
As a result of the present strike at least two shipping companies have moved their lifters and transporters by train, in one case to Halifax and in another to Saint John, New brunswick. The Canadian Importers Association has now advised its contacts and its principals in Europe and elsewhere in the world to re-route cargo into Montreal by methods other than the maritime method, at least from now until the beginning of September.
We in the Montreal region are in the midst of a crisis which I do not think too many of our citizens yet appreciate. We have tended to have strikes and see them settled on a more or less acceptable basis over the years. I submit this situation is more dangerous than any I have witnessed since I first entered the House of Commons in 1963.
The situation, as I read it, has deteriorated to the point where the employers, in agreeing to this three-year contract, have tied themselves into a fairly expensive provision of annual wage guarantees to the dockworkers. It would appear the employers now find themselves in a position where, even if the port is immediately reopened, they will be in serious financial difficulty. Ships have left, they have been turned away, and ships headed here have been diverted elsewhere. The employers would find themselves in extremely serious financial circumstances in maintaining the financial terms of the contract they entered into if the men were to go back to work tomorrow.
The background of this dispute is still not completely clear to me or, I suggest, to anyone else. There are a number of factors affecting the union's attitude and a number affecting the employers' attitude. From my understanding of the situation, there is a considerable amount of fault on both sides to this dispute. In most instances this is the case. There are usually two sides to the story and the Montreal strike is no exception. There is serious fault, in my view, on both sides and there is no inclination that I can see by either party to take the measures, open and incumbent upon them under the law, to submit to arbitration.
Given these circumstances, I say to the government there is no longer any choice. It must, in my view, adopt more than the passive role it has taken up to now. The Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) has acted correctly in saying to the parties that under the law he cannot force them to enter into arbitration. He has pleaded with them to do so. He has asked both sides to submit to the legal method available to them to resolve their disputes. But both parties have refused.
We have waited for several weeks for a move, but nothing has happened. We can no longer allow the business atmosphere of Montreal to be poisoned or the future of the port to be permanently damaged. I was not surprised, but very depressed this afternoon when I heard members from western Canada more or less write off the port of Montreal. The message is clear; people are writing off the port of Montreal and its future. The port of Montreal is far too important to Canada as a whole to be written off.
The two parties to this dispute appear unwilling or unable to make a move. The government, in the public interest, must now move into the situation and by legislation if necessary and trusteeship if necessary force a conclusion to what is now occurring in Montreal. As a general rule, the federal government in its labour relations suggests it does not believe in the idea of stepping into labour disputes because such action tends to prolong the dispute and the parties wait until the government steps in to solve things for them. They decline their responsibilities when there is a hope that the federal government will step in.
As a general principle I accept this as a logical and good argument, but in this instance I feel a number of factors have entered into the situation which make it unlikely that either party will take the initiative in instituting arbitration proceedings. That being the case, there is no choice and we should step into the picture. If nothing happens between now and Monday, I say to the Minister of Labour, through you, Mr. Speaker, that we must think in terms of legislative action.
The malaise which is the principal topic of the debate today, the strike, is not the only ill which affects the future of the port of Montreal. During the past year and a half we had high hopes that with the establishment of a new port authority there would be more rapid movement toward resolving some of the problems which have been plaguing the port of Montreal. This movement, however, still is not visible. The creation of the port authority took much longer than had been expected. When it was finally set up-I believe about six, eight or nine months ago-we were led to believe we would see some fairly rapid results of its activities.
So far we have not even seen a movement toward some of the activities for which a number of interested people in Montreal have been pushing for at least 12 years, such as an analysis of the land owned by the port with a view to developing the Montreal port to its maximum economic use. We find there are areas belonging to the port of Montreal which are underused in comparison to their economic possibilities. There is the question of whether or not the port of Montreal, in order to fully develop, should

June 16, 1972

expand across the river into the south shore area from Boucherville down river.
There is a question which bothers me considerably in respect of this possible port expansion. I refer to the question of what will happen to the Boucherville Islands immediately in front of Boucherville. These islands have been partly acquired by the port of Montreal. In my view they are an ideal site for recreational activities for the population of the eastern part of Montreal particularly. I have argued that the port of Montreal should move directly to the south shore rather than to these scenic islands which have tremendous recreational possibilities for a population which at the moment does not have major recreational facilities available to it.
Not only the port of Montreal, but in fact all our eastern ports are in desperate need of promotion. The major ports around the world sent emissaries to all world trading centres with the objective of bringing trade to these ports. Montreal, Halifax, Saint John and all our major eastern ports are in need of a much more effective promotion policy. In my view this has been a serious deficiency which reflects on the effectiveness of our National Harbours Board. The National Harbours Board has been sadly remiss in this area.
I understand there are now some moves afoot to correct the lack of commercial acumen which this government organization has demonstrated for so long. Hopefully, once a promotion is under way it will benefit not just one port but the entire eastern seaboard of Canada. With an excellent work force, efficient shippers and shipping agents we are in a position to compete very effectively with the United States ports which are now busy taking business away from the three Quebec ports which have been tied up by this most unfortunate strike.
One further point I feel should be made this afternoon is that the new Montreal port authority when it was set up was given a fairly flexible framework so far as membership is concerned; the number was not tied down completely. However, only one member on the labour side of the picture was appointed to the port authority. I would recommend strongly to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) and the Minister of Labour that the labour representation on the Montreal port authority be increased. Perhaps I am engaging in wishful thinking, but it seems to me that had this been the case and had there been additional labour representation on the Montreal port authority, it would perhaps have been able to play a more effective role than it has in the resolution of the very grave labour difficulty which has afflicted the port of Montreal for the past number of weeks.
In closing, I urge again that the Minister of Labour at the beginning of next week, if there is no sign of improvement or movement, take the necessary steps to bring the parties together into arbitration if they will agree, and if they will not agree then I suggest we have no alternative but to consider establishing a trusteeship for the port of Montreal.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having on many occasions during the past few weeks put several
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
questions to the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) concerning the longshoremen's strike in Quebec ports, and as the representative of an electoral district near the port of Montreal, I take pleasure in participating in this afternoon's debate on this unfortunate strike, which has lasted far too long.
Mr. Speaker, we are faced with an illegal strike where the parties refuse to resort to arbitration or to meet, and on the other hand the minister tells us that although procedures are clear there has been no request for arbitration.
Faced with such a conflict and such confusion, the federal Minister of Labour, however, is also unable to claim that he cannot take action by hiding behind procedure as everyone agrees that the strike, which is indeed very serious, has lasted long enough, that losses on all sides, both to workers and employers in Quebec and Canada, are huge. It is time an end is put to the conflict and that a settlement takes place.
I should like to give a chronological outline of this strike which I followed, long and short, from the start.
On March 27, the officials of the employees union and of the shipowners accepted, on principle, a collective agreement. On April 4, this agreement was submitted to and practically unanimously accepted by longshoremen by a vote of 2,400 to 6.
On April 19, after acceptance of the agreement by the longshoremen, the federal government mediator, Mr. Poirier, who is an excellent mediator, a capable person, personally prepared, drafted and finalized the collective agreement which was signed by employers and employees in his presence.
All went very well until May 9. The agreement was signed on April 19, and it does not seem to me that there were problems until May 9, that is, nearly three weeks after the agreement was signed.
But on May 9, at eleven o'clock in the morning, there was a walkout in Montreal and other Quebec harbours for no known reason. The longshoremen walked out at eleven o'clock on May 9 for no known reason. But a few days after this walkout took place, we learned that it had been called out of sympathy for the leaders of the Common Front of Labour.
In relation to this walkout, the shipowners obtained an injunction and the longshoremen had to go back to work on May 10. On May 11, everyone was back to work and at 2 o'clock in the afternoon, the shipowners, or management, learned from the unions that they had violated section 9(11) of the collective agreement only three weeks after its signature.
This section had to do with the employment of men in the holds or on the decks of ships or in the warehouses in the harbours of Quebec.
When for example an employer needs 16 men to load or unload a ship, they make up a gang. When eight members of the team are working on the bridge and four in the hold-that is 12 men out of 16-four remain idle on the bridge or in the hold. Now, Mr. Speaker, the employers hired them to work at something else in the sheds. The unions would like those four men who belong to the gang

June 16, 1972
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike to remain idle, on the wharf or on the bridge while under the collective agreement, the employers can make them work in the sheds. It seems that such is the clause at stake in the present strike.
Mr. Speaker, while everybody was at work on May 12 and 15, meetings were held in the presence of the federal conciliator. The union leaders stated: "Injunction or no injunction, we will disregard any legislation and we refuse arbitration". This is quite different from what my hon. colleagues were saying a moment ago: "They refused arbitration because the conflict in connection with Subsection (11) of Section 9 cannot be subject to arbitration". They claimed that they would close the ports, and this is effectively what has happened. The strike has been on since May 15.
For the past month, approximately 500,000 tons of goods have been lost and I regret to say that Canada must depend for supplies on foreign shippers who look after the transportation of our goods, as Canada does not have her own merchant marine as yet.
We are now facing the following situation: the longshoremen are on strike and the shipowners have no more shipping to do. They are facing this dilemma whereby a collective agreement has just been signed which guarantees job security for the employees. Therefore, in what way could the employees be given job security in the future when the ports of Quebec remain idle, ships have gone away and there would be no work if the strike were settled? The shipowners are facing the following problem: that is to guarantee job security whereas they have no work to offer.
Mr. Speaker, this is a case where the minister must take action and must intervene. Once the strike is settled-I hope it will be soon-it will take from eight to ten weeks before the situation becomes normal in the Quebec ports generally or in the port of Montreal. That is to say that it will take from eight to ten weeks to have enough merchandise to load or to unload so that longshoremen will have some work to do.
I say it again, shipowners have signed a collective agreement which guarantees job security whereas, because of the strike, they have no work for the longshoremen.
Under these conditions, Mr. Speaker, there is a procedure to be followed. There is a solution. It is no more a matter of arbitration, because one of the interested parties has clearly said that it had no faith in arbitration and that it would not use it.
Now there cannot be any arbitration if both parties are not there.
When arbitration is impossible, one has to or resort to mediation. And the Minister of Labour should step in as early as next Monday and ask both parties to come to a settlement.
And in order to make mediation easier, the Minister of Labour for instance could ask both parties to suspend the somewhat embarrassing clause on job security, for eight to ten weeks, so that the situation may go back to normal in the Quebec ports and especially in the port of Montreal, so that ships may come back to our ports, that work may be resumed and that employers may guarantee job security as was provided for in the collective agreement.

The Minister could even offer to guarantee the longshoremen income security for 8 to 10 weeks, and if they do not want to lose their pay for not having worked during the strike, the federal government could, through a mediator, offer them income security until the situation goes back to normal and the provisions of the collective agreement concerning job security are in effect again.
However, arbitration has turned out to be impossible, so far. However, next week we could put an end to the strike, and I suggest we allow the Minister of Labour this time to resort to mediation and bring both parties to their senses.
But the Minister of Labour cannot hope to solve this dispute by simply inviting both parties to come to an agreement without offering them some concessions.
If arbitration does not work out next week the Minister of Labour could submit to the House a bill to settle this dispute.
Mr. Speaker, in closing, I must say that there have been enough pleas. Parliamentarianism as well as negotiations in the House have lasted long enough. Enough questions have been asked the Minister of Labour. It is high time for action and I hope that next week the Minister of Labour will step into the second stage in the settlement of this dispute by doing everything he can to bring both parties together and by making, in the name of the federal government, offers likely to help in settling this problem.
All of us will be happy if, through arbitration, we reach a settlement of the dispute. In case of failure, we will be glad in this House to study any legislation to put an end to it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul St. Pierre (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO SETTLE QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention in this debate will be brief. I shall deal with just one point which has been raised by several of the members who have spoken, including the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell). It is central to the question of compulsory arbitration in strikes which affect the public interest.
The point which more than one hon. member has touched upon is that in certain areas of the Canadian economy, in which both management and labour know that the service which their industry provides is vital to the economy, there is a continuing tendency for both sides to enter so-called negotiations from extreme positions, in the full knowledge and expectation that they will eventually reach compulsory arbitration imposed by the government, if necessary by act of Parliament.
For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I think it might be generally agreed that often such negotiations are not conducted seriously or in very good faith because arbitration, by its very nature, becomes mere compromise. It isn't greatly different from what we call mediation. And when the point is reached at which arbitration is imposed, the arbitrator in fact is in a position of finding a middle line between the opposing positions.
Therefore, not only in this strike in the port of Montreal, in which of course the parties have not yet been brought to the point of arbitration, but in railway disputes and other disputes affecting the national interest I suggest to
June 16, 1972

the House that our present system encourages the two parties, management and labour, to stay apart rather than to come together.
It discourages serious bargaining, because if one party or the other acts in the pretty sure appreciation that eventually they are going to go to arbitration, and in the pretty sure appreciation that most arbitrators do little more than find a middle line between the extremes, its interests obviously for its own group, whichever side it is representing, management or labour, is to begin from the most extreme point.
For this reason I want to put before the House today a bill which has been before the United States Congress this year. Without saying that I endorse it, I would say that it is imaginative; and I would think that in labour negotiations in Canada, particularly in areas such as the dock strike, we need some imagination. I would like to discuss briefly the form and content of this bill. It is a Senate bill, S.3232, and was put forward by 29 Senators headed by Mr. Pack-wood. The bill is dealing specifically with strikes similar to the Montreal dock strike. I quote from section 208(1) dealing with a strike which-
-affects an entire industry or a substantial part thereof engaged in trade, commerce, transportation, transmission, or communication among the several states or with foreing nations or engaged in the production of goods for commerce-
It is a lengthy bill. It provides for cooling-off periods and for various other forms of labour negotiations with which we are familiar. But there is one specific section of the bill which I wish to draw to the attention of the House. It appears at page 13 and is entitled "Final Offer Selection." This may not be new to some hon. members, but it is new to me and I find it a most intriguing proposition.
Essentially, the proposition is that before arbitration is imposed in a strike in the United States affecting the national interest in the areas I have quoted, each party would be obliged to make a final offer and one alternative final offer. The major and significant difference which this bill proposes from anything which we know in Canada is that the arbitration board, chosen in the normal manner-a three-man board-would not have the choice to alter final offers; it would be obliged to select holus-bolus one or the other. I would like to read these sections, Mr. Speaker, and I think I can do it quite quickly. Section 219 reads:
The President may direct each party to submit a final offer to the Secretary of Labor within three days. Each party may at the same time submit one alternative final offer. The Secretary of Labor shall transmit the offers to the other parties simultaneously.
(2) If a party or parties refuse to submit a final offer, the last offer made by such party or parties during previous bargaining shall be deemed that party's or parties' final offer.
Quebec Longshoremen's Strike
(3) Any offer submitted by a party pursuant to this section must constitute a complete collective bargaining agreement and resolve all the issues involved in the dispute.
(b)	The parties shall continue to bargain collectively for a period of five days after they receive the other parties' offers. The Secretary of Labor may act as mediator during the period of the final offer selection proceedings.
(c)	If no settlement has been reached before the end of the period prescribed in subsection (b) of this section, the parties may within two days select a three member panel to act as the final offer selector. If the parties are unable to agree on the composition of the panel, the President shall appoint the panel.
There are other subsections here which I will not read, but subsection (g) provides:
The panel shall at no time engage in an effort to mediate or otherwise settle the dispute in any manner other than that prescribed by this section.
Subsection (j) provides:
Beginning with the direction of the President to submit final offers and until the panel makes its selection, there shall be no change, except by agreement of the parties, in the terms and conditions of employment, and no strike, lockout, or similar activity shall take place. In no instance shall such period exceed 30 days.
(k) The panel shall not compromise or alter the final offer that it selects. Selection of a final offer shall be based on the content of the final offer and no consideration shall be given to, nor shall any evidence be received concerning, the collective bargaining in the dispute, including offers of settlement not contained in the final offers.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that is ap imaginative approach which is worthy of the consideration of the House. If, on reflection, the two parties to a dispute recognize that in going before an arbitrator they must arbitrate not merely a middle line between opposing positions but put forward a final offer and win everything or lose everything, it seems to me that both parties, management and labour, would be obliged to consider seriously the provisions contained in their final offers because they would know that compromise is not the solution since they will stand to win or lose everything.
